#6418. New underwater discoveries in Australia show how First Peoples lived before the ocean swallowed their land

Divers found 21 stone tools on the seabed off Australia, including some made of stone carried 14 miles to a freshwater spring that is now 40 feet under water.

The seabed off a coast looks like the last place an archaeologist would dig. Yet when the last Ice Age ended and the oceans rose, the coast people had lived on for tens of thousands of years went under, stone tools and all.

Off northwestern Australia, divers have now found 21 stone tools on the seafloor. They lie at two spots that were dry land until about 9,000 years ago.

Almost half the tools at one site were made of a rock from an island at the far edge of the archipelago.

That rock outcrops only about 14 miles (23 kilometers) away. Someone carried that stone across a landscape that is now open water. Its destination was a freshwater spring that now lies 40 feet (12 meters) down.

Jonathan Benjamin, a marine archaeologist at Flinders University, led the work, with colleagues at the University of Western Australia, James Cook University and the University of York.

Rangers from the Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation dived alongside them, and two are co-authors on the research paper. The scientists state that they can’t date the tools directly, so 9,000 years is a floor, not an age.

The Ngarda-Ngarli people have cared for Murujuga, also called the Dampier Archipelago, for at least 50,000 years. It was listed as a World Heritage site in 2025. On land it holds more than 4,000 recorded sites, from stone scatters to rock art.

The first underwater finds there came in 2020. The two new sites extend the record offshore and down.

One is a submerged freshwater spring in Flying Foam Passage, about a quarter mile (400 meters) from today’s shoreline. It is a depression 525 feet (160 meters) long, with rock walls up to 8 feet (2.5 meters) high.

The other is a boulder-strewn knoll called the Maitland River Hummock. It is on the bank of a drowned river channel, nearly a mile (1.3 kilometers) from the nearest island.

Both sites were drowned by the same rising sea, roughly a thousand years apart. The knoll would have been a small, rocky island by about 10,000 years ago and was under water soon after.

The spring went under around 9,000 years ago, when rising seas spilled over the sill at the passage’s northern end.

Divers worked the sites on neap tides, when currents in the passages are weakest, for about 40 minutes per dive.

Every rock is coated in marine growth. A diver had to judge shape and angle by eye, lift a candidate stone tool, and send it up.

At the spring, eight dives produced 158 rocks hauled to the surface. After a soak in diluted acid to strip the growth, nine proved to be artifacts: three whole flakes, five broken ones, and a core with at least 12 flake scars.

Most of what a diver lifts turns out to be just a rock.

The knoll was richer. Fourteen dives there produced 12 artifacts, including two cores from which 16 and 19 flakes had been struck.

Murujuga Ranger Malik Churnside, trained as a scientific diver, found one of the knoll’s artifacts himself. Two of the 21 pieces are not pictured in the paper, at the direction of Murujuga Elders.

“The collaboration demonstrates the value of working beside trained Indigenous Rangers who actively contributed to this challenging scientific research,” Benjamin said.

The team read each stone tool’s chemistry with a handheld X-ray fluorescence scanner. Two elements, titanium and zirconium, were plotted against the known rock types of the archipelago. The signal survived thousands of years under the sea.

At the spring, 56 percent of the tools were the local granophyre, a granite-like rock found on both sides of the passage. The other 44 percent were a volcanic sedimentary rock that, today, outcrops only on or near Rosemary Island, about 14 miles (23 kilometers) away.

The knoll told a different story. All 12 of its tools were local rock, probably quarried from the outcrop itself or from an island 2 miles (3.5 kilometers) north.

So the spring looks like a gathering place, where people arrived carrying tools made elsewhere. The knoll looks like a quarry beside a river.

On land, nearby sites that became islands when the sea rose show mostly local stone, which fits a world where the long walks had ended.

The artifacts lie loose on the seafloor, with no buried layers or charcoal to date. Their true age could be anywhere from 9,000 years back to the 50,000-year record of the wider region.

Their edges are slightly rounded by sand, but current meters show the tides move sand, not rocks this size.

The samples are small, 12 tools at the knoll and 17 at the two spring sites. An unmapped outcrop of the island rock could also sit closer on the seabed than the geology on land suggests, though the team considers the known map reliable.

Vincent Adams, director of the Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation, said the finds change the map of what needs protecting.

“What this research shows is that our cultural landscape extends far beyond the shoreline and into Sea Country, where important parts of our story remain preserved beneath the sea,” he said.

Everything found so far lies inside the 100-foot (30-meter) depth contour. The drowned coast runs out to about 425 feet (130 meters), where the oldest material should be.

Reaching it will take bigger boats and faster ways to tell a tool from a rock. The team wrote that both are on the agenda.

The full study was published in the journal Quaternary Science Reviews.

#6417. Scientists Ranked 20 Protein-Rich Foods on Health, Affordability, and Sustainability. One Surprising Food Came Out on Top

Tofu took the crown in a showdown of 20 protein-rich foods judged on health, affordability, availability, and their toll on the planet.

Protein-rich foods can look very different when cost, access, health, and environmental impact all enter the picture. In a study published in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, Dr. Chris Macdonald developed a framework that combines these four considerations to compare commonly consumed protein sources.

Among the 20 foods assessed, tofu took the top spot, while cheddar cheese finished last. The results followed a clear pattern: plant-based foods occupied the entire highest-scoring fifth, and animal-based products made up the lowest-scoring fifth.

Tofu’s lead came from strong results across both parts of the assessment. It earned a perfect 16 points for environmental performance, placing in the best-performing fifth for greenhouse gas emissions, water pollution, land use, and freshwater use. It also scored 20 out of 24 points for health and accessibility, including full marks for providing all nine essential amino acids.

Together, these measures explain why the rankings go beyond protein content alone. They weigh the environmental costs of producing protein alongside nutritional factors and practical considerations such as price and availability.

The paper argues that ratings focused on one feature can leave consumers with an incomplete picture. A product’s performance in one area does not explain its trade-offs elsewhere. Macdonald presents the framework as a way to help people understand those competing considerations and the food systems their purchases support.

As the paper states, “Against deliberate corporate obfuscation and marketing myths, the goal of a holistic score is not to create a new label, but to foster a new literacy, one that empowers us to see the reality of the systems we are funding.

Ultimately, beyond the spreadsheets and scores, lies a fundamental reckoning: our protein choice is a referendum on the compassion we are willing to show to animals, to the planet, and to future generations.”

The research builds on Macdonald’s work at the Better Protein Institute, which examines how much protein people need for optimal health, how to shift consumer behavior effectively, and where investment could support future protein sources. By questioning common assumptions and starting from first principles, that work addresses some of the most frequently Googled questions about dietary protein.

Reference: “What are the best sources of protein? Introducing the BPI Score” by Chris Macdonald, 1 July 2026, Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems. DOI: 10.3389/fsufs.2026.1677796

#6416. People lost the same amount of weight drinking water or diet beverages in a two year study

A two-year study of 493 adults showed that people lose about the same amount of weight whether they drink water or diet beverages.

If you are trying to lose weight, choosing diet drinks over water will not make a huge difference. In a two-year study of 493 adults, participants who drank diet beverages and people who drank water showed very similar weight loss results.

All participants followed a weight-management program and drank at least two 11-fluid-ounce (330-milliliter) servings a day of their assigned drink.

Those still enrolled at two years had lost 10.6 pounds (4.8 kilograms) with diet drinks and 8.2 pounds (3.7 kilograms) with water.

The difference between the groups was not statistically significant. Only 220 of the 493 participants completed the trial.

The SWITCH trial was run at the University of Liverpool in England. Participants lived within 50 miles (80 kilometers) of Merseyside and began their trial drinks between July 2016 and December 2021.

The trial enrolled adults aged 18 to 65 with a body mass index of 27 to 35. They were randomly assigned to water (246 people) or diet drinks (247 people).

Their average age was about 45, and roughly seven in ten were women. The investigators supplied the drinks, which the sponsor paid for.

The diet group chose from 20 branded beverages containing the artificial sweeteners aspartame, acesulfame potassium or sucralose. The water group drank bottled spring or mineral water and was asked to avoid diet drinks.

For 12 weeks, participants attended weekly group sessions led by nutritionists. Monthly sessions followed for 40 weeks, and the final 52 weeks were unassisted.

Advice covered healthy eating and cutting sugar. During the first year, participants were also asked to add ten minutes of daily walking until they reached 60 minutes on six days a week.

The main analysis covered the 220 people with weight data at both the start and week 104. Of those, 117 drank water and 103 drank diet beverages.

Two other analyses that accounted for dropouts also found no significant difference. One used multiple imputation, and the other carried forward each person’s last recorded weight.

After the first 12 weeks, weight loss was equivalent with either drink. Water drinkers had lost 12.3 pounds (5.6 kilograms) and diet-drink users 12.8 pounds (5.8 kilograms), a 2023 report on the trial found.

At one year, diet-drink users had lost significantly more weight in the main analysis, though the gap was not clinically meaningful. By two years, the gap was no longer significant.

Professor Jo Harrold, dean of psychology at the University of Liverpool, led the trial.

“These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomised trial,” Harrold explained.

Waist and hip measurements fell in both groups, with no difference between them.

Total cholesterol rose more with diet drinks. Blood sugar, measured as HbA1c, and diastolic blood pressure fell more with water, but none of these differences was judged clinically meaningful.

Hunger rose slightly over two years, whichever drink people had. The increase was significant only in the diet-drink group, and the difference between groups was not significant.

Sugar intake fell with either drink, slightly more with diet beverages. Total sweetener intake fell significantly only among water drinkers.

Professor Jason Halford, a co-author at the University of Leeds and the University of Liverpool, pointed to the length of the trial.

“This study provides the long-term clinical evidence that has been missing from international discussions,” Halford said.

In 2023, the World Health Organization advised against using non-sugar sweeteners (NSS) to control body weight. The recommendation was conditional and does not apply to people who already have diabetes.

The guideline covers sweeteners such as aspartame, sucralose, saccharin, stevia and acesulfame potassium.

It drew on a systematic review that found no long-term benefit for reducing body fat. Possible long-term harms in adults included higher risks of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and death.

“Replacing free sugars with NSS does not help with weight control in the long term,” said Francesco Branca, WHO’s director for nutrition and food safety.

The SWITCH authors argue that the guidance rests mainly on uncertain findings from cohort studies rather than randomized trials.

“We hope this evidence informs future WHO guidance and public health policy,” Harrold noted.

The authors partly blame the low completion rate, about 45 percent, on the COVID-19 pandemic, the two-year length and the voluntary final year. That final year was added by amendment after recruitment fell short.

The trial took place at a single site in England, and data on race and ethnicity were not collected.

About 76 percent of participants already drank diet beverages regularly before joining. The trial compared diet drinks with water, not with sugary drinks.

The American Beverage Association funded the research. The team states that it was independent of the funder and fully controlled the analysis and reporting.

The funder could review the manuscript, though final decisions on content rested with the authors. Several authors also report funding from or ties to beverage or food industry organizations.

The study was published in the journal British Journal of Nutrition.

#6415. Cancer Immunotherapy Has a Dangerous Side Effect. Scientists May Have Found a Way To Stop It

Cancer immunotherapy could become safer by stabilizing the cells that keep immune responses under control, an approach that reversed treatment-related inflammation in mice.

Some cancer patients have to stop immunotherapy when their immune system starts attacking healthy tissue. These reactions can occur with drugs called immune checkpoint inhibitors, which help immune cells known as T cells fight cancer by releasing the brakes that normally restrain them.

Depending on the type of checkpoint inhibitor, 20% to 40% of patients experience these immune-related adverse events. Up to 25% experience severe reactions that result in hospitalization and an end to treatment. There are no U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved treatments for these side effects.

“Immune-related adverse events are a huge problem and can greatly impact quality of life for patients. In many cases, it impacts their ability to stay on immunotherapy or benefit from treatment,” said Abigail Overacre-Delgoffe, Ph.D., assistant professor in the Department of Immunology at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and a member of the Tumor Microenvironment Center at UPMC Hillman Cancer Center.

Overacre-Delgoffe is the senior author of a study published October 22, 2026, in Cell that identifies unstable immune cells as a potential driver of this inflammation. Her team reversed inflammation in mice by blocking a protein in those cells and found that diet and the gut microbiome, the community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract, influenced the severity of the animals’ reactions.

Studying these side effects has been difficult because they vary considerably among patients. Animal models have also struggled to reproduce the complexity of immune-related inflammation in humans.

“Most existing mouse models relied on genetically modified mice or experimental conditions that didn’t really capture the variability we see in patients,” said lead author Dipyaman Patra, Ph.D., a postdoctoral associate in Overacre-Delgoffe’s lab. “This got us thinking about whether common lifestyle factors, particularly diet and the gut microbiome, could influence the host immune system even before immunotherapy begins.”

Overacre-Delgoffe’s earlier work had shown that diet and gut microbes can influence cancer patient outcomes and responses to immunotherapy. To investigate their role in treatment side effects, her team fed mice a diet designed to resemble a Western-style human diet, low in fiber and high in fat and processed carbohydrates. The animals began eating it two weeks before checkpoint inhibitor therapy and continued during treatment.

The mice became susceptible to immune-related adverse events and developed immune and microbiome changes resembling many of those seen in affected patients. This gave the researchers a way to test how gut microbes contributed to the inflammation.

Transferring fecal microbes from mice eating the Western-style diet into mice eating a regular, high-fiber diet caused gut inflammation in the recipients. Transfers could also reduce inflammation. Male mice were less susceptible to severe adverse events, and transferring their fecal microbes into female mice reduced the severity of inflammation in the females.

The team also transferred fecal microbes from patients consuming a Western-style diet into germ-free mice, which are raised without microorganisms. Those recipients developed more severe immune-related adverse events. Together, the transfer experiments provided evidence that the microbiome could influence the severity of these reactions in mice.

Within the immune system, the researchers identified a problem involving regulatory T cells. These cells normally suppress excessive immune responses, but stress can make them unstable, a condition called regulatory T cell fragility. Mice eating the Western-style diet showed signs of this fragility during immunotherapy. The researchers found the same instability in regulatory T cells collected from patients with severe immune-related adverse events, but not in cells from patients without the side effect.

Blocking an immune-signaling protein specifically on regulatory T cells restored their stability in mice and reversed inflammation. Switching the animals to a high-fiber diet or giving them supplements containing metabolites, substances produced through metabolism, also stabilized the cells. Restoring stability significantly reduced the severity of adverse events, supporting the interpretation that regulatory T cell fragility is a major underlying cause in this model.

“We were able to generate the first of its kind preclinical mouse model of adverse events that didn’t require full gene knockouts,” said Overacre-Delgoffe. “By combining this novel preclinical model alongside patient data, we were able to identify a very new mechanism of adverse events that hopefully will result in new targeted therapies, allowing more cancer patients to stay on treatment and out of the hospital.”

The model will give researchers a platform to investigate why some patients develop severe reactions and to identify biological markers that might predict susceptibility. Future work will explore drug targets in specific tissues that could limit or eliminate these side effects without disrupting immunotherapy. Metabolite supplementation is another potential approach to reducing susceptibility without interfering with the microbiome, although its promise here comes from experiments in mice.

“We now have some potential targets that we’re going after that seem to limit immune-related adverse events without negatively impacting immunotherapy, which would be the first of its kind and is quite exciting” Overacre-Delgoffe said.

Reference: “Lifestyle-induced regulatory T cell fragility primes adverse events after immune checkpoint blockade” by Dipyaman Patra, Katelyn Wolfgang, Chenxian Ye, Lora Rigatti, Kelsey Ertwine, Kristin M. #6414. Many physicists now believe that gravity and the fabric of the universe are just a giant web of connected quantum information

Two physicists derived Einstein's equations of gravity from a measure of quantum information, a new clue in the search for quantum gravity.

If you open any physics textbook, it will tell you that gravity is one of the four fundamental forces of nature. However, two scientists have just shown that Einstein’s math for gravity can actually be explained by something that isn’t a force in the first place.

They start with a measure of how easily they can tell apart a patch of space holding matter and a patch of empty space.

If the argument holds, the curving of space and time isn’t a starting point. It is a consequence of how quantum information is arranged.

Philipp Dorau and Albert Much of Leipzig University in Germany published the work in March. It is a mathematical argument, not an experiment, and it rests on simplifying assumptions the authors spell out.

“It is a little like plucking a guitar string: matter is the pluck, spacetime is the string, and the note it produces is Einstein’s equations,” said Much, an assistant professor of quantum field theory and general relativity and a co-author of the study.

In 1995, the physicist Ted Jacobson showed that Einstein’s equations could be derived from the physics of heat and entropy.

The laws describing a gas emerge from the motion of its molecules. Gravity, he suggested, might emerge from something deeper in the same way.

Jacobson’s version used classical thermodynamics, the science of heat flowing between warm and cold things. Dorau and Much wanted the same result using only quantum field theory, the mathematics that describes matter at the smallest scales.

For that they needed a different kind of entropy. The usual quantum measure of disorder gives infinite answers for a sharply defined region of space, because entanglement between neighboring points never stops at small scales.

The quantity they used instead is called relative entropy. It measures how well two quantum states can be distinguished from each other, and it stays finite.

Here is one way to picture it. Imagine the surface of the sea, which is never perfectly still. Its constant rippling is like the quantum vacuum, the state physicists call empty space.

Now imagine a wave passing across that surface. Relative entropy tells you how well you can distinguish the wave from the rippling background.

The two physicists worked out this quantity at a horizon. Any small patch of curved space contains one, in the form seen by an observer who keeps accelerating.

“We show that this quantity, evaluated at a horizon – a boundary in spacetime beyond which no information can be received – equals the energy flowing across that horizon,” Much said.

The last step borrows a rule from black holes. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking argued that the entropy of a black hole grows with the area of its horizon rather than its volume.

Dorau and Much assume that same entropy-area rule holds for their local horizons. Relative entropy equals the energy crossing the horizon, that energy sets how much the horizon’s area changes, and Einstein’s equations follow with no extra ingredients.

With the black hole value for that rule, the usual constant in front of the equations comes out right. Furthermore, second free constant appears, which the authors identify with the cosmological constant.

However, the authors are careful about what they have shown. “Most of the ingredients for our work have been known for decades,” said Dorau, a theoretical physicist at Leipzig’s Institute for Theoretical Physics.

“It was recent progress in understanding relative entropy that gave us the missing link between quantum information, thermodynamics, and gravity.”

The derivation treats matter in its simplest form, as the smallest possible disturbance of empty space. It works only to a first approximation.

The paper says a fully rigorous treatment would have to track smaller corrections, which the authors expect to be technically demanding.

It also leans on the equivalence principle, Einstein’s rule that any small enough region of curved space behaves like flat space. And the entropy-area relation at the heart of the final step is assumed, not derived.

What comes out at the end is the semiclassical form of Einstein’s equations, in which spacetime stays classical while matter is quantum.

That isn’t yet a theory of quantum gravity, the long-sought merger of Einstein’s gravity with quantum theory. Furthermore, whether the same reasoning survives when matter takes more complicated forms is still an open question.

The two physicists plan to try. They want to extend the argument to other kinds of quantum matter, to more general quantum states, and to light-like surfaces, which are central to black hole physics.

“We are currently trying to generalize this to full quantum gravity, and it seems to me that this connection that we have identified will serve as a testbed for the various theories of quantum gravity,” Much said.

The full study was published in the journal Physical Review Letters.

Julie Elie, an ethologist at the University of California, Berkeley, tells Live Science's Kenna Hughes-Castleberry about using AI to decode the vocalizations of zebra finches.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Bird calls are far more than pleasant sounds in nature. They are complex forms of communication that can reveal how birds think, learn, cooperate and respond to their surroundings. From intricate songs used to attract mates to alarm calls that warn others of danger, vocalizations offer valuable clues about avian intelligence and social organization.

Julie Elie is an animal behavior researcher and associate project scientist at the University of California, Berkeley. She recently won the 2026 Coller Dolittle Challenge for Two-Way Interspecies Communication for her work in studying and deciphering zebra finch communication.

For more than a decade, Elie observed the social behavior of birds, recording thousands of sounds and using machine learning combined with behavioral experiments to decode specific calls.

In this interview, Elie discusses how zebra finches learn and use vocalizations, what their calls reveal about intelligence and social relationships and how artificial intelligence (AI) contributed to decoding birdsong.

Dr Julie Elie is a computational neuroethologist who studies how social animals communicate. Her research combines behavioral experiments, neuroscience, and computational tools to reveal how animals produce communication sounds, what information they transmit in their vocalizations and how they perceive the meaning of vocalizations.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: What made you study birds and birdsong?

Julie Elie: The beginning of my work with birds dates from my Ph.D. I've always been super interested in animal behavior in general. But I think as a young person, I was more attracted by animals that we relate more easily to, which are mammals, right? Dogs, cats, horses.

I wanted to do a Ph.D. on animal behavior and, more specifically, on relationships between animals. I was interested in how animals interact with each other and what kind of social organization they establish.

[Someone suggested I] work on the zebra finch, and I said, "OK, I've never taken the time to really observe birds very well; might as well start now."

I realized that it's difficult to observe birds because they're not close to you. They can fly wherever they want. When you are out and about in town, in the countryside, and you see birds, they're here, and then they're gone. You don't get to see a lot of their vocal interactions or a lot of their social interactions.

So here I was, studying the zebra finch in cages where they were fully interacting with each other. And the question was, what kind of social organization do they have?

I realized quickly that they were not doing a dominance hierarchy [which was previously thought to be the case], but instead, the most important thing in their life was their partner. They were doing pair bonds, and that's the core of their social organization, [with] males and females pairing for life.

Studying birdsong can help researchers like Elie better understand how the birds navigate their complex environments.

KHC: Why is it important to study birdsong, and what can it teach us about intelligence and behavior?

JE: A level of complexity we were trying to understand was, what are the neural mechanisms that enable those birds to do this process of listening to something and copying it, and reproducing it, and doing a comparison between what they're producing and what they're hearing?

The zebra finch is a just-right middle ground level of cognitive ability that is interesting, where you see this pattern of copying vocalization and producing it. But you can look through the avian kingdom, and some species show more complex behaviors.

We know that there are some species that are able to not only imitate their own vocalizations from their own species, their dad, but they're able to copy other species. So, here in California, for instance, a mockingbird is a bird that is really known to be able to reproduce a bunch of different sounds and is actually incorporating this in their vocalizations.

Parrots are also well known for that because we have them as pets, and they're able to reproduce our own vocalizations as humans. This is kind of crazy, when you think about it, because they don't have the same vocal tract as we do. It's smaller, and they have a different system. I think a high cognitive level is when an animal is able to reproduce a sound that is not in their "native language," let's say, and use it for a goal. We do see this in parrots ‪—‬ they're able to ask you for something or even ask the dog to shut up sometimes, which is interesting. They're able to really use those vocalizations, such as "This is not mine, but I communicate with another species this way."

It shows you how smart they can be, and by studying vocal communication in animals, we are getting a window of what cognitive abilities they have and how the usage reveals their level of smartness.

KHC: Could you walk me through how you ended up decoding bird vocalizations?

JE: I spent countless hours observing zebra finches, and I realized that I could progressively do a match between the social context and the acoustic characteristics of the sound produced. I could recognize these sounds and understand what they "mean."

It's like at home with your cat or dog: Within a couple of months, you figure out every time the cat is doing this kind of sound —‬ "meow" — ‬it means he wants to get out or he's hungry, or he wants to cuddle. Same thing with the dog. It's the same process, but instead of doing this with cats or dogs, I did this with birds and constituted the first acoustic dictionary of zebra finch calls.

However, how do you know you are correct? That you correctly identified the sounds that correspond to the "words" in that species?

Pet owners can often differentiate between different vocalizations in their pets, such as different meowing noises for their cat.

I thought that the best confirmation of whether I was right or not could only come from the zebra finches themselves. Up to now, nobody had found a way to systematically go through the vocal repertoire of an animal and confirm if each identified call type was indeed perceived as a word in that species' language.

To achieve this somewhat impossible discussion with a bird, we designed an operant conditioning experiment where the bird is asked to classify vocalizations that were previously recorded from other zebra finches. The game is simple and relies on two rules. The first one is that every day, only the recordings corresponding to one call type are rewarded by seeds, while the recordings from the other call types in the repertoire are not rewarded. The second rule is that the bird can interrupt recordings and skip to the next one whenever they want, like how you skip through songs on your favorite music app.

The bird is placed in a cage that has a button or a little infrared sensor that it can activate with its beak. Each time it does so, the recording of a vocalization randomly drawn from the library of call types is played. Four out of five times, birds trigger the playback of a call type that will not give them access to seeds. Because they are slightly food deprived, they only really want to listen to the rewarded playback, so they interrupt the nonrewarded calls and only listen for the calls that are going to be rewarded.

Every day, the bird has to find out which call type or "word" is rewarded. They usually figure it out pretty rapidly and then start interrupting the playback of all the other call types. Using this task, we could test a different call type every dayIf they had not been able to do it, it would tell us that the call type we had identified was in fact not existing in their language. If they were able to do it ‪—‬ and spoiler alert, they were! ‪—‬ it meant that we had correctly identified that call type.

The birds told us yes, basically —‬ the organization that you're proposing is correct.

But then we made a surprising discovery. We noticed that birds were making some rare and systematic mistakes. We wondered if these mistakes were coming from the acoustic similarity of the call types — how you might mistake, for instance, the word "glove" for "love" or "hurt" for "heart." Or if they were coming from the semantic similarity of the call types — you could maybe mistake "love" for "heart" if you are remembering about the general meaning of the rewarded word today, which is "love.".

In that last case, it would mean that birds truly have an understanding of their call types' meaning. We found out that birds' errors could be better explained by the meaning [the semantic similarity] of the call types. That is a big discovery in the field of animal communication.

I'm thinking that the first species we might be able to communicate with, interact with vocally, might be a bird.

KHC: Do you think we are headed toward actually being able to communicate with birds, or do you think it's more that we're still testing the waters and we still need to learn the rest of the language before we get there?

JE: When we say "talking with birds," I think we need to understand that it's not going to be a language. Right now, I am studying the zebra finch; it doesn't mean that I would be able to communicate with a crow once I have a repertoire. So there's this component of when we talk about birds, there are many different species.

I think there's more traction in this particular part of the animal kingdom than in other parts, just because birds are really talkative. Birds use a lot of their vocalizations to communicate with each other. So because of that, I'm thinking that the first species we might be able to communicate with, interact with vocally, might be a bird, just because they are very talkative.

For now, I found all those words. But we need to understand how those words are [strung] together. So it's not necessarily the case that we need to understand the rules of the dynamic exchanges between individuals or how fast you're responding, but how you are responding and whether that makes sense or not.

They [also] have [body] postures. They have specific displays at the same time they're producing the vocalizations. And if we really want to achieve full communication with another species, we need to get to that level.

It's not tomorrow for sure, it's probably not next year, but I think in the range of 10 years we should get there. Especially with how fast the domains of AI and robotics are. I have some hope that we should be able to get to that point.

KHC: Is there one takeaway you would want our readers to know about your work?

JE: Just one. The most important thing for readers that are not specifically scientists is to realize that, by studying animal behavior more generally, researchers are discovering the intelligence of animals. This is opening our eyes to other species and realizing that we're not the only species that is intelligent on this planet.

This is a lesson to us as another species on this planet, that we are not the only ones that are smart and we need to take this into account in how we are evolving.

We need to realize how we're affecting them and realize that they also have their own internal lives, and maybe we should start to respect them a little bit more.

Editor's note: Some of this interview was conducted via email as part of a follow-up conversation. The interview has been edited lightly for clarity and length.

#6411. More Than a Billion Years of Earth’s History Is Missing – Scientists May Finally Know Why

Earth’s rocks are missing more than a billion years of history in some places, and the slow rise and fall of continents may explain how those chapters disappeared.

A study led by University of Wollongong (UOW) PhD candidate Santosh Dhungana suggests that the slow rise and fall of continents helped create the Great Unconformity, a vast gap in Earth’s geological record. Published in Nature, the research links this missing history to currents of hot rock in the mantle that moved continents vertically over hundreds of millions of years.

Normally, rock layers preserve a sequence of events, with younger deposits accumulating above older ones. At the Great Unconformity, that sequence jumps: sedimentary rocks from around the beginning of the Cambrian period, roughly 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite more than a billion years old.

“Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth’s story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren’t lost by chance,” Dhungana said.

The Grand Canyon exposes one of the most striking examples of this geological gap. It lies within what was once the ancient continent Laurentia (modern North America). Similar boundaries appear in Europe, Australia, Africa, and Asia, although the missing intervals vary from about 200 million years to well over a billion.

Explaining the Great Unconformity requires accounting for both the removal of rock and the survival of the eroded surface beneath younger deposits. Dhungana said that although scientists had offered several explanations, those ideas had not been thoroughly tested against Earth’s behavior over time.

To investigate, he and his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, modeled mantle convection across hundreds of millions of years. The mantle consists of hot, solid rock that flows very slowly. Its currents can gently lift enormous stretches of land or allow them to sink.

The models indicated that mantle currents raised the ancient continental cores of Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe), and North China during the Neoproterozoic Era, from about one billion to 540 million years ago. This prolonged uplift would have exposed rock to erosion. The era was followed by the Cambrian period, when animal life diversified dramatically.

The next stage helped preserve what erosion had left behind. During the Phanerozoic eon, which spans the past 540 million years, the continental cores gradually sank. Seas spread across their worn surfaces, and accumulating sediment buried the boundary between the ancient rocks and the younger geological record.

The modeled pattern matched the geography of the evidence. North America, northern Europe, and North China, where the Great Unconformity is especially well preserved and documented, all showed the prolonged rise followed by sinking that the researchers proposed.

“Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface,” Associate Professor Flament said.

“Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed, but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle.”

Reference: “The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity” by Santosh Dhungana, and Nicolas Flament, 4 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11156-5

This study was funded by the Australian Research Council.

#6410. Fake rocks are helping rare Australian snakes survive in the wild after builders took their natural homes

At least four out of six broad-headed snakes, raised in captivity then released under artificial rocks, survived their first months.

For years, people have taken natural sandstone from the Australian bush for landscaping. This practice leaves broad-headed snakes without homes.

To address the problem, scientists released six captive-bred snakes back into the wild in May 2026, giving them human-made rocks to live under.

According to the University of Technology Sydney (UTS), this world-first release is working, with at least four of the snakes surviving their first few months.

Six animals is a tiny sample, the count is preliminary, and neither official announcement cites a published or peer-reviewed paper. Yet the scientists behind the study are encouraged.

UTS wildlife ecologist Jonathan Webb leads the program with Aussie Ark and the Traditional Owners of the Shoalhaven. His own field site is a population in Morton National Park, south of Sydney, and he has been counting snakes there for 34 years.

Webb started on the snake during his PhD at the University of Sydney. The species had once been common around Sydney. By the 1990s it was rare, while other snakes were doing fine.

He kept monitoring after the PhD and joined UTS in 2012. “It turned into a long-term study purely by accident,” he said of the 34 years. Internship students still go out with him on the surveys each year.

The snake has a flattened head and a black body with yellow bands, and it grows to about 35 inches (90 centimeters). It lives only on the rocky escarpment of the Sydney sandstone basin and the ranges around it.

Its life runs slowly. A broad-headed snake can take five years to reach adulthood. Females reproduce only every two or three years, and wild adults can reach 23.

Young snakes depend on rock outcrops for shelter and for food, because they eat only small rock-dwelling lizards such as geckos and skinks. Webb said that removing the rocks takes away both.

The state of New South Wales listed bushrock removal as a key threatening process in a final determination dated November 5, 1999. The document names Hoplocephalus bungaroides, the broad-headed snake, among the threatened animals affected.

Webb said the rules need enforcing. He wants a permit system that makes sellers prove their rocks did not come from areas with threatened species.

Landscape suppliers still sell boulders taken from the bush, he said, and a feature boulder can fetch 450 Australian dollars. He called that “really frustrating.”

Weather and fire added to the damage. His monitoring recorded a decline during the 2017-19 drought. Little breeding followed for three years after the 2020 bushfires. By 2023 the population had dropped by around 64 percent.

Aussie Ark secured 17 wild adult snakes in October 2024 to start the captive side of the program. That group later grew to 20 and lives in terrariums at Conservation Ark in Somersby, New South Wales.

Earlier in 2026 the program recorded the first captive birth of the species, Aussie Ark said. A few weeks later, remote-sensor cameras filmed a live birth, which the group described as never documented before.

Eight juveniles have been bred so far. Two stayed in the captive group because of their genetics, and six went to the release sites. Aussie Ark project lead Dylan Wallis and Chief Conservation Officer Hayley Shute let one of them go together.

Each snake carries a unique marking on its head, so staff can identify individual animals during later checks. Captive programs are helping other Australian species too. The University of Newcastle reported a first captive breeding of Littlejohn’s tree frog.

Dr. Benjamin Croak, who completed his PhD at UTS under Webb, developed the artificial rocks. UTS says they have the right crevice size and mimic the thermal properties of natural stone.

The snakes hunt at night and spend the day under rock, which gives them warmth and cover and also draws the lizards they eat, Webb said. He described the artificial versions as “critical to the survival of the juvenile snakes.”

Croak had worked on the species’ shelter needs years earlier. In a 2013 paper in PLOS ONE with Webb and Richard Shine, he reported radio-tracking nine adults in Wollemi and Yengo national parks.

The snakes spent most of winter beneath sun-warmed rocks. The authors recommended that managers keep existing surface rock in place.

The program also trains and supports Indigenous rangers to monitor the snakes on Country. Traditional Owner Frank Connolly Jr. said the snake is “important to our culture” and that young people are learning the work for the next generation.

UTS, in its note of November 6, says at least four of the six survived the first few months. That is the only survival figure in the official announcements. Aussie Ark’s release note says the six went out under artificial rocks but gives no survival count.

The figure is a minimum from a very small group, a few months after release. UTS says Webb’s team has run fortnightly surveys. Neither note gives the survey results or the date each snake was last seen.

The announcements also describe no comparison group of snakes released without artificial rocks. Webb’s view that the rocks made the difference therefore remains an expert judgment, and UTS still calls the release a pilot study.

Predators are an early risk. Webb named kookaburras and brown snakes among native hunters, along with invasive cats and foxes. In South Australia, researchers confirmed that feral cats killed 74 of 389 reintroduced animals at two sites.

Breeding in the wild is further off. Adulthood can take five years, so the released juveniles have a long wait before they can add to any population. Pressures on snakes worldwide, such as habitat loss, continue in the meantime.

Webb said the focus for the next few years will be restoring habitat and releasing more captive-bred snakes at selected sites. Aussie Ark founder Tim Faulkner said the group had spent years “navigating so much red tape” to reach the first release.

One of Webb’s first memories is sitting on his dad’s shoulder while the kid next door let him touch a green tree snake. Going out to check the young broad-headed snakes under their artificial rocks, he said, “I feel like a kid again.”

The information was obtained from the University of Technology Sydney.

#6409. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

#6407. ZWO Seestar S30 Plus review

We tested the brand-new ZWO Seestar S30 Plus, an all-in-one smart telescope for beginners and hobbyists that makes astrophotography accessible to everyone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's much to enjoy about the Seestar S30 Plus. The image quality is great, it's easy to use, and it's compact and lightweight enough to take it anywhere. It's not quite as good as the more expensive S30 Pro, but it's a nice middle-ground option between the S30 and the S30 Pro that gives you a lot of features for the money.

Seestar app is reliable and easy to navigate

All-in-one workflow from shooting to sharing

2K image quality is better than we expected

Editing controls could be a little more responsive

Not suitable for smaller planetary nebulas

Why you can trust Live Science Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best ones for you. Find out more about how we test.

ZWO has just released the newest member of its smart telescope range: the Seestar S30 Plus. This all-in-one smart telescope is designed for beginners and hobbyists who want an affordable way into astrophotography that won't leave you scratching your head, and lets you capture, process and share your images in one simple workflow. It sits between the Seestar S30 and S30 Pro, and is priced at $499 for its release.

With 2K image quality, a light pollution filter and a user-friendly interface, it's a smart telescope that anyone can enjoy, regardless of your experience level, and regardless of whether you're shooting from your city balcony or a dark sky site. Like the other models, it uses dual cameras to capture a wide range of subjects, including deep-sky objects with the telephoto camera, and constellations, star trails and the Milky Way with the wide-angle camera. It's lightweight and easy to travel with, and it even comes with a separate solar filter for solar imaging and eclipse time-lapses.

We got our hands on an advance copy to test ahead of its release, so we put it through its paces on several different celestial subjects.

The Seestar S30 Plus is one of the smallest, most compact smart telescopes on the market, weighing just 3.63 pounds (1.65 kg) and measuring 8.3 x 5.5 x 3.2 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm). Its sleek, matte white design looks identical to the other Seestar models (we compared it to our S30 Pro), except for the branding on the unit itself.

It comes in a padded soft carry case and includes a small tripod (although we always prefer to use our own), a solar filter, a 40-inch (1 meter) USB-A to USB-C charging cable, a removable shoulder strap for the carry case, and a quick-start guide. With its accessories and case, the whole setup weighs 4.89 pounds (2.22 kg).

On the unit itself, you'll find just one button, which powers it on, plus the USB-C port on the side. Super simple, although we'd have liked the USB-C port to be covered to prevent moisture or dust from getting in.

It comes with a carry case, strap, USB-C cable and solar filter.

The set-up process couldn't be easier. When you turn the telescope on, you'll hear a double beep and see the power button light up alongside the red dots on the black screen to indicate the battery level. Four dots mean the battery is full. The telescope will tell you when it's ready to connect, at which point you can sync it up to the app on your smartphone or tablet. To turn it off, you just select "Shutdown" in the app, which closes the arm and turns the unit off.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It also features an anti-dew heater, which we've found works quite well in mild to moderate humidity. On a couple of our shoots, we noticed a tiny bit of condensation forming on the unit when the humidity was higher, so we wouldn't feel confident leaving it unsupervised for long periods on a particularly dewy evening. (We used the Clear Outside app to monitor the humidity levels.)

The Seestar App is user-friendly and easy to navigate, with just the right amount of controls: you have plenty of options to choose from but it doesn’t become overwhelming. The main Seestar page is where you'll likely spend most of your time, as this is where you can search for celestial objects to shoot, access your album, plan a shoot and read up on what objects Seestar recommends based on your time and location.

The Stargazing section is where you can select or search for the subject you want to shoot. You can use the search function to find a specific target or browse Tonight's Best, and you can also search through different types of subjects like galaxies, nebulas, clusters and more. From here, you can also select planets, track comets and photograph constellations using the wide camera.

Click on a subject and the app will display information about it, including its current altitude and coordinates, which help determine what time is best to shoot that particular object. It automatically applies the appropriate filters and settings, but you can override these if you want to.

There's very little to complain about when it comes to using the app. It has lots of information for beginners, so you don't need a ton of knowledge about the night sky, and everything is fairly self-explanatory. There were a couple of occasions when it failed to calibrate itself (for example, when we tried to locate the Pleiades, which had just risen above a tree), and other times when we chose a new target and it slewed the long way round instead of only having to move slightly. But otherwise, the app worked well.

The AI Enhance section has some good editing tools to bring out the best from your photos. You can reduce the stars, adjust the brightness, contrast, saturation and RGB curves, apply denoise and eliminate any satellite trails — although we'd love a dehaze slider to bring out some of the fainter nebulosity of certain objects. The sliders could do with being a little more responsive, especially the RGB curves, but overall, it does a pretty good job of editing your pictures to get a pleasing result.

We had about 10 days to test our review unit before its release, so we could only capture as much as the weather permitted in that time. We'll add more images to this review over the coming weeks. All our tests were conducted from our backyard in a Bortle 4 region, and captured before moonrise to eliminate as much light pollution as possible. Due to these time constraints, we aimed to capture our images for a total of 60 minutes each, although we'd have ideally aimed for longer in some cases.

Now for the fun part — the images. The Seestar S30 Plus has a focal length of 160mm, which is advantageous for capturing large subjects like the Andromeda Galaxy, the North America Nebula and the Pleiades. Large emission nebulas are where it really shines; however, the focal length is too short to capture smaller apparent objects.

For this review, we aimed to capture as many different types of objects as possible. All our images were edited in the Seestar app with, in some cases, a few minor tweaks in Lightroom. You also have the option to download the individual files to your computer to process them yourself in dedicated astrophotography software, which is advantageous if you're a more experienced user.

Everyone's favorite star cluster, the Pleiades, was one of the first targets we wanted to capture. We could see the faint blue nebulosity after as little as 15 minutes of integration time, and it only improved over time. After 60 minutes, we had a really nice image and could easily bring out the blue haze via the editing tools in the app. However, we got a much more impressive result after tweaking our image a little further in Lightroom, bringing out even more haze and reflective dust.

The Andromeda Galaxy is a perfect target for the Seestar S30 Plus. It takes up a large portion of the frame, and with long integration times, it can reveal beautiful details in the faint outer arms. We shot for around an hour in our tests due to weather and time constraints, but we still got an impressive image. As we approached 60 minutes, there was a lot of cloud cover, and we noticed it struggling to stack images toward the end of the session, so we stopped the integration at 57 minutes.

Andromeda is certainly going to be the most impressive galaxy for the Seestar visually, as most others will appear smaller in the frame and will need longer integration, so make sure you have a clear, dark night for it.

Large emission nebulas are where the Seestar S30 Plus thrives, and the North America Nebula is a great target. It covers the whole field of view, and the red hydrogen gas easily comes to the forefront of the image.

The Eastern Veil Nebula is another lovely target where you can bring out the beautiful red and turquoise hues in as little as 15 minutes, but longer integration times will yield brighter, more colorful results.

Planetary nebulas are where you will see the limitations of the Seestar's 160mm focal length. Most planetary nebulas have a very small apparent size — we've previously captured the Dumbbell Nebula and Cocoon Nebula with our S30 Pro, and they were a tiny dot in the middle of the screen. We tried the Helix Nebula, and even though it's one of the largest apparent planetary nebulas, it's still fairly small on the Seestar S30 Plus. You can still get a decent image of it, but if you want to focus on imaging planetary nebulas, you'll need a bigger scope. Because it was very low in the sky and there was some interfering cloud, we stopped integration at 27 minutes.

The Seestar S30 Plus is an affordable entry point into deep-sky astrophotography without the confusing settings and expensive setup. It's ideal for beginners, although more experienced users will likely want to upgrade to the superior image quality and extra features of the S30 Pro.

Still, for under $500, we can't complain. Not only is the Seestar S30 Plus easy to navigate and use, but it teaches you about space in a fun and interactive way, and you don't need to spend hours stacking individual frames on your computer to process — although you still can do that if you want more control over your editing.

If you can stretch your budget, the S30 Pro is a worthy upgrade. It produces 4K images and offers more pro-level features.

To see deeper into space, the Seestar S50 Pro has a longer focal length of 260mm and a larger 50mm aperture, making it better for smaller apparent objects.

If the imaging aspect doesn't interest you, the Celestron StarSense Explorer range of telescopes connects to your phone to guide you around the sky, but you observe the cosmos through an eyepiece instead of capturing it on your phone.

Read our full Celestron StarSense Explorer LT 70AZ review

Kimberley Lane, E-commerce writer for Live Science, has tested a wide range of optical equipment, reviewing camera gear from Sony, Canon, OM System and more. With over 6 years of photography experience, her skills span across landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in a number of national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan. She has also contributed to our sister site Space.com and Tech Radar, and she regularly uses binoculars and telescopes to stargaze in the dark skies of South Wales.

#6406. A tiny ocean animal called the leaf sheep figured out how to make its own food from sunlight

The leaf sheep is a sea slug that looks like a cartoon lamb standing in its own pasture. Oddly enough, the pasture is the strange part. The leaf-shaped…

The leaf sheep is a sea slug that looks like a cartoon lamb standing in its own pasture. Oddly enough, the pasture is the strange part.

The leaf-shaped growths on its back are green because the slug keeps chloroplasts, which are the sunlight-capturing parts of the algae it eats. Those chloroplasts go on working inside the leaf sheep for days or longer.

Animals eat food for energy, and plants make their own food from sunlight. A few sea slugs do both, and the best-studied one is a bigger cousin of the leaf sheep, Elysia chlorotica, an emerald green slug from the Massachusetts coast.

In 2008, researchers found one clue to how it manages that, in its own DNA: a working copy of a gene taken from the algae it eats.

The leaf sheep’s scientific name is Costasiella kuroshimae. It is about the size of a grain of rice, according to the World Wildlife Fund, and lives in shallow tropical water around Japan, Indonesia, and the Philippines.

Two ear-shaped feelers above its eyes sense chemicals in the water, and it grazes on an alga called Avrainvillea on shallow reefs and in seagrass beds. The species was first described in 1993.

Mary Rumpho at the University of Maine led the work on the cousin with James Manhart of Texas A&M University. Their team went looking in the slug’s genes.

A chloroplast carries only a small part of its own instructions. Of the 1,000 to 5,000 proteins a chloroplast needs, its own DNA codes for fewer than 10%. The rest come from genes in the algal cell’s nucleus.

So a slug that keeps the chloroplast and loses the rest of the algal cell should end up with chloroplasts that can’t maintain themselves.

E. chlorotica keeps them anyway. A gene passing between an alga and an animal is extremely rare, or at least not well documented, and Rumpho’s team set out to find one.

The slug hatches from eggs that carry no chloroplasts, and its larvae swim free. They won’t change into juveniles without one alga, Vaucheria litorea, which grows in long threads, and the juveniles must feed on it to keep developing.

Young slugs are grayish brown. As they feed, they keep chloroplasts only in the cells lining their branched gut, and as that gut spreads, the whole animal turns green.

The chloroplasts never divide inside the slug, which lives about 10 months. In earlier work, Rumpho’s group had measured oxygen coming off slugs kept from algae for at least five months. The chloroplasts were still photosynthesizing.

The team started with the alga. They read the complete DNA of its chloroplast and found that one gene was missing. It was a gene called psbO.

That gene makes a protein that the photosynthesis process requires in order to split water and release oxygen. Sunlight wears that protein out, so a chloroplast has to keep making more of it.

The algae plant keeps this gene in its main control center, not in the chloroplast. Until now, scientists had never seen an animal naturally possess this gene.

So if the slug’s chloroplasts were still releasing oxygen five months after their last meal of algae, the protein had to be coming from somewhere. The team looked in the slug.

They found the gene there, matching the algal version exactly, and it was switched on.

A leftover bit of algae in the slug’s gut could explain that. So the team checked slug eggs, which carry no chloroplasts and no algae. The eggs had the gene too.

That was the team’s evidence that the gene belongs to the slug itself and gets passed on to its young.

Rumpho’s team also sequenced the slug’s mitochondrial DNA, the small, separate genome that animals carry in their cells. The gene wasn’t there, which left the slug’s nuclear DNA as the likely location.

How did the gene get there? The authors suggested a route. When the slug feeds, algal nuclei come into direct contact with the cells lining its gut.

If a nucleus breaks open there, pieces of algal DNA could be taken up by the slug, or carried across by a virus.

Other algal genes have turned up in the slug too. A year earlier, another group had reported three algal genes in E. chlorotica that code for proteins that help collect light, matching the alga’s almost exactly.

The authors also wrote that the slug adds weight to an idea from biologist Lynn Margulis. New kinds of life, she proposed, can arise when one organism takes in parts and genes from another. They called slugs like this “green animals.”

The team did not find where in the slug’s chromosomes the gene is, what DNA surrounds it, or what switched it on once it arrived. They also did not learn how the protein gets from the slug’s cell into the chloroplast.

The authors wrote that many more algal genes have very likely been transferred to the slug. Reading its whole genome is what it will take to settle where they are.

The study did not ask any of this about the leaf sheep. The next question is whether Costasiella carries an algal gene of its own, and its genome is the place scientists should look next.

The full study was published in the journal PNAS.

#6403. An ancient Roman settlement missing from all history books was found in a Welsh village right before new houses were built

A survey taken before the planned construction of 300 homes at Mancot in Wales led archaeologists to a 2,000-year-old Roman settlement.

In December 2025, archaeologists from Heneb were working on a housing site beside Gladstone Way in Mancot, a village in Flintshire, northeast Wales. Castle Green Homes planned to build 300 houses on the land.

The ground on that plot held a Roman settlement that was completely unknown, never mentioned in historical records.

The site is about 2,000 years old and produced an unusually large collection of Roman metalwork. Heneb published photographs captioned as a Roman brooch casting mold from the dig, and the finds are still being analyzed.

The development is called Gladstone Grange, and Flintshire Council had allocated the land for housing. The developer assessed the site for archaeological value before the project began and hired Heneb, the Trust for Welsh Archaeology, as part of that process.

A geophysical survey, which maps buried features without digging, picked up structures and signs of historic activity under the ground. Heneb then monitored the site before and during the early stages of the work.

The trust says it completed a full investigation of the remains before the site was developed. It announced the find on November 9, 2026, and said the fieldwork has ended.

Excavators uncovered a Romano-British industrial settlement, the term archaeologists use for communities in Britain under Roman rule. It sat inside a network of plot boundaries and drainage systems.

A site plan released by Heneb marks groups of buildings lettered A to H. A large drainage ditch formed the eastern boundary for most of them.

The settlement grew in phases. Timber houses came first, and Heneb says some of them may date to the end of the Iron Age.

By the third century AD, elongated, semi-rectangular buildings had replaced those houses. One photograph from the dig shows the outline of a third-century building in the cleared soil.

Heneb thinks the remains continue west under the part of the village now called Big Mancot. The announcement does not say how far they run.

Heneb lists a wide variety of brooches from Mancot. People in Roman Britain pinned their clothes with them and also wore them as decoration.

The trust published photographs of the objects. One shows a disc brooch set with enamel. Heneb says the decoration appeared only after extensive laboratory conservation.

Another photograph shows an enamelled brooch of the Wirral type. A third shows a large brooch of a kind often found on Anglesey, the Welsh island where detectorists recovered fifteen Iron Age gold coins.

The dig also produced a lead spindle whorl, a weight for spinning thread. A denarius of the emperor Commodus turned up too, and Heneb’s caption dates it to AD 192.

Three more photographs carry the caption “Casting mould of a Roman Brooch.” Heneb does not say whether they show one mold or several.

Heneb says “substantial evidence” suggests the inhabitants made these brooches themselves. The trust thinks they probably worked within “a wider industrial supply network” that served local people and Chester.

Mancot overlooks Chester, site of the Roman legionary fortress of Deva Victrix. Romans built it in the AD 70s and occupied it for more than 300 years. The Twentieth Legion was based there for most of that time, according to Cheshire West and Chester Council.

Very little Roman activity had been recorded in this part of Flintshire. Heneb says the land around Chester has often been described as a “largely undeveloped hinterland,” which is why the trust considers Mancot significant.

Other industrial sites had already turned up elsewhere in north Wales. At Pentre Ffwrndan, near Flint, Roman workers smelted lead ore from Halkyn Mountain from about the mid-60s AD. The former Clwyd-Powys Archaeological Trust, now part of Heneb, says it is likely the lead was shipped to Chester.

Volunteers and archaeologists working there in 2017 and 2018 excavated a Roman road aligned toward a probable quayside on the estuary.

At Prestatyn, bronze smiths, iron smiths and enamellers worked in adjacent timber workshops from about AD 90 or 100 until about AD 160, the national record of Welsh monuments says. A trust leaflet adds that excavators there found slag, bronze scrap and parts of casting molds.

Near Wrexham, a detectorist’s lead ingot led researchers to the first confirmed Roman villa in North Wales. Another detectorist in the region found up to 15,000 Roman coins.

Heneb places Mancot within this emerging pattern and argues that Roman Wales was “far more complex and interconnected than previously understood.”

Heneb’s announcement gives no total for the brooches, the coins or the buildings. It also does not mention furnaces, hearths or metal waste at Mancot, the kinds of remains reported at Prestatyn.

The link to Chester remains an inference, and Heneb words it as a probability. The trust has named no buyer, and the announcement cites no chemical test that ties the metal to the fortress.

The objects are undergoing analysis and conservation. They will then go to Flintshire Museum Services, which plans a public display, though Heneb has given no date.

Heneb has finished digging at Gladstone Grange, where 300 homes are being built. The brooches, the casting finds and the Commodus coin stay with conservators for now.

The information was obtained from Heneb: The Trust for Welsh Archaeology.
