#6402. A last minute skeleton discovery finally proved that a Norse church once stood right near Erik the Red’s Greenland settlement

A skeleton found at Qinngua confirms the first Norse church found in Greenland in over 60 years.

In August 2026, archaeologists at Qinngua, near Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland, reached the second-to-last day of their planned excavation timeline.

The National Museum of Denmark first dug at this particular ruin in the 2000s, and none of the work since then had turned up a burial site. Until that fateful day.

Their skeleton discovery confirms that the stone ruin was a Norse church, the first found in Greenland in more than 60 years. Its date is still provisional, and researchers are analyzing samples from the site.

Qinngua lies close to Brattahlíð, the main settlement of Erik the Red. Researchers from Copenhagen’s National Museum worked there with Bergen’s University Museum, Greenland’s National Museum and Archive and UNESCO Kujataa.

Michael Nielsen of the Greenland museum photographed the dig, and Kujataa site manager Aqqaluaq Frederiksen shot the ruin from above.

The ruin consists of a rectangular stone wall with a stone building in the middle. Researchers had suspected a church there for some time because of that layout, which the University of Bergen calls a typical mark of a medieval church.

According to the National Museum’s history pages, Greenland’s oldest churches were small, stood close to farmhouses and had circular churchyard walls. Farmers built them and owned them.

Proof needed a cemetery with graves. Museum teams dug at Qinngua in the 2000s and found none.

This summer the team located a skeleton placed with its head toward the east, which the museum describes as customary for Christian burials. The grave confirmed a cemetery, and the cemetery confirmed the church.

Christian Edelfelt Koch Madsen coordinates research on the project for the National Museum. He called the grave “the smoking gun.” He said, “Now there is no doubt that this is a church.”

Inuit were buried in stone-covered chambers and Norse people in cemeteries, Madsen said, and the written sources point the same way.

Konrad Smiarowski of the University Museum of Bergen co-leads the project. He said in Bergen’s statement that the Norse dead lay in consecrated ground beside churches.

The end of the dig drew many curious locals from the village of Qassiarsuk, according to a caption in the museum’s press pack.

Medieval texts name several Norse churches and say roughly where they stood. Smiarowski said researchers have placed most of them using those texts, especially Flateyjarbók and Ívar Bárðarson’s description of Greenland, along with landscape analysis and known Norse settlements.

One account mentions Kirkja undir Sólarfjöllum, the Church under the Sunny Mountains. The National Museum said this description fits Qinngua rather well.

The mountains behind the site stand right by the ice cap, under a local high-pressure system that often brings sunny weather. The site is in the part of Tunulliarfik Fjord that the Norse knew as Eiriksfjord.

Madsen expects the match to guide future fieldwork. Because this location agrees with the sources, he said, “it would make sense to try to locate other churches also mentioned in writing.”

Researchers have found six churches in the relatively small area around Brattahlíð, and only three remained in use into the Middle Ages. The ruins of two or three farms stand near the new church, which may suggest the beginnings of a village.

The National Museum’s research page on the Norse says farms with a church were central places in a hierarchic society. Other farmers were probably tied to church owners through kinship, religion or tenancy.

Madsen said the cluster near Erik the Red’s seat looks like “a veritable race to build churches and thus demonstrate power and position.” Some builders may have lost that race and given up on their churches, he said, and Qinngua could be one of them.

Smiarowski described churches as centers of power as well as places of worship. Studying them, he said, can show how Norse society handled climatic and social pressures.

Churchyards have been informative in Denmark too, where 77 Viking graves clustered around the lost St. Oluf’s Church in Aarhus.

The Norse held on in Greenland from about 980 until the 1400s. Written sources say Icelanders led by Erik the Red settled the southwest around 985, and that the Western Settlement emptied in the middle of the 14th century.

The last written evidence of life in the Eastern Settlement dates to 1408. Archaeological finds and radiocarbon dates suggest people stayed there until at least the middle of the 15th century.

A Norwegian king appointed a bishop for Greenland in the early 1100s, the National Museum says, but bishops probably did not reach their post at Gardar until the early 1200s. None lived there after Bishop Alf died in 1378.

The churches found 60 years ago dated to the Viking Age and were soon given up. The Qinngua church is bigger and was likely used through the Middle Ages, a period when knowledge is “still full of holes,” the National Museum said.

Lake sediment work has tied the arrival and departure of the Greenland Norse to shifting temperatures. Hemlock and jack pine from five Norse sites in Greenland also point to timber trips to North America.

The institutions have not published a laboratory date. The range of 1100 to 1300 comes from the church’s large size and its many hewn stones, and the arms laid along the sides suggest the early Middle Ages.

The statements describe one skeleton and give no age or sex. They also give no measurements for the building. The announcement came as a press release, without a peer-reviewed paper.

Neither statement reports an inscription or object that names the church, so the link to Kirkja undir Sólarfjöllum rests on the landscape.

The two possible histories of the building also remain open, since the museum describes likely use through the Middle Ages while Madsen suggests its owners may have abandoned it. “More research will show,” he said.

The grave confirmed on that second-to-last day is the the first burial reported at Qinngua at Qinngua. Samples from the find are still being analyzed.

The information was obtained from the National Museum of Denmark.

#6400. New laser mapping tool helps scientists track baby trees and monitor forest regrowth on a massive scale

Culling deer let 2.65 million young trees spread across the Cairngorms, and a laser scan from a plane mapped Scotland's forest recovery.

The Cairngorms, in Scotland’s Highlands, are famous for bare, heather-covered hills. Those hills used to be forest. Woodland once covered half to four-fifths of the country, but only about 4 percent of the native forest is left.

Across one stretch of the Cairngorms, though, the forests are coming back on their own, and a plane carrying a laser scanner has now counted them.

The scan found 2.65 million young trees under 16 feet (5 meters) tall across 220 square miles (569 square kilometers).

About 13,000 acres (5,325 hectares) of open ground now carries enough saplings to count as young woodland. Very little of it was planted. The land managers shot deer instead.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge led the mapping, with partners at RSPB Scotland and Cairngorms Connect, the partnership that manages the land. Sudina Thapa and Aland Chan were the first authors.

The scan is a single snapshot of trees, commissioned in July 2023, and the smallest seedlings, the ones still hidden in the heather, are not in the count.

In an interview with Earth.com, Chan said the scale was what surprised him. “You notice regenerating trees on the ground, but that feels very different from seeing millions of trees plotted on the map,” he said.

Four land managers formed Cairngorms Connect a decade ago, with a 200-year plan to let native forest climb back up to its natural tree line inside the Cairngorms National Park.

Their main tool is culling deer, which eat seedlings before the seedlings can get established. Ecologists have estimated that deer numbers have to fall to roughly 3 to 5 per square kilometer, about 8 to 13 per square mile, before young trees can regenerate.

Across the partnership, densities now average below 4 per square kilometer. That is the threshold the whole plan rests on, and the hills have crossed it.

Young woodland here means more than 100 trees per hectare, about 40 per acre. Of the 6.17 million trees the scan picked out, 43 percent were under 16 feet tall.

The authors wrote that this colonization was largely natural, with small areas of planting where no seed trees were nearby.

Mapping trees from the air with laser scanning is not new. The LiDAR scanner fires pulses at the ground, times the return of each one, and builds a three-dimensional picture of everything below.

This flight, about 2,000 feet (600 meters) up, recorded 22 pulses for every square meter of ground.

The hard part was the small trees. Heather in these hills grows to about 3.6 feet (1.1 meters), and bracken grows taller, so a young pine can be shorter than the shrubs around it.

“We’re not the first study to use LiDAR to map trees, but it’s the first time we’ve used it to map these small, regenerating trees at this scale,” Chan told Earth.com.

The team’s method found trees once they outgrew the heather. Checked against Cairngorms saplings measured on the ground, it caught 83 percent of tree clusters between 4.6 and 5.2 feet (1.4 to 1.6 meters) tall. Above 6 feet (1.8 meters) it caught more than 95 percent.

Trees still under about 3.3 feet (1 meter) were almost all missed.

With every young tree on a map, the team could ask where the forest is spreading and where it isn’t. Distance from existing forest mattered most. The farther a patch of ground was from a seed source, the fewer saplings it held.

Bogs consistently held fewer young trees than dry heathland. Elevation made little difference low down but was more important above about 1,300 feet (400 meters), where the ground approaches the natural tree line.

Where deer had hit hardest in the past, fewer saplings stood now. Parcels rated low or medium for browsing damage in surveys run between 2006 and 2013 carried more young trees than parcels rated high.

One oddity stood out. The parcels rated very high carried more saplings than those rated high. The authors suggested heavy browsing may have opened up the vegetation and exposed bare ground for seeds.

Chan said ecologists have long known that trees regenerate less readily far from seed sources or on boggy ground. Putting a number on how much less, he said, is what makes it possible to model what happens next.

Asked by Earth.com what walkers in the Cairngorms should notice, Chan said Scots pine tends to come back first, with birch and rowan following. A self-seeded forest grows differently from a plantation.

“Instead of dense rows of trees of roughly the same size shading out the entire understory, visitors will see trees of different shapes and sizes scattered across the landscape,” he said.

That mix of shapes and sizes creates more kinds of small habitat for animals, he added.

Capercaillie, a large grouse, and red squirrels are among the species now confined to the remaining fragments of old pine forest. More woodland is more room for them.

Pip Gullett of Cairngorms Connect, a co-author, said the method is also good at tracking the effects of fires, which are growing more severe with climate change.

Field crews from the partnership and RSPB Scotland had already surveyed parts of the landscape on foot. The laser count of land with more than 100 trees per hectare came out in the same range as those ground estimates once a correction was applied.

Field crews who measured saplings a year later found them slightly taller than the laser had. A batch of 136 Scots pines averaging 7 feet (2.1 meters) tall had grown about 7 inches (17.6 centimeters) in that year. Seedlings still below the heather line remain uncounted.

Rocks and clumps of bracken can be mistaken for trees, and the authors filtered them out using color images taken on the same flight. The method has only been tested at this one site, with this one scanner and flight height.

The Scottish Government is now commissioning a laser scan of the whole country. The authors wrote that their approach could be scaled up to build a national record of woodland expansion.

Chan said the next thing he wants to map is the shrub layer itself. Dozens of species depend on the heather and blaeberry, he said, and that layer sets much of the fire risk.

Until that map exists, the count stops at the trees tall enough to clear the heather.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Applied Ecology.

#6399. This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The ancient creature differs from all other known amphibians in its ability to tolerate saltwater

A Gerrothorax maritimus fossil unearthed in China was discovered in an ancient seabed, suggesting it's the first and only amphibian known to have lived in the ocean.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

A fresh look at Einstein's equations suggests that gravity can sometimes snap and reconnect, similar to magnetic field lines on the sun. The findings hint at a new way that gravity and matter can trade energy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Magnetic reconnection — the process behind the sun's most violent outbursts — may have a counterpart in gravity.

According to a new theoretical study, sheet-like structures in the gravitational field can break apart and reconnect in new arrangements, much like the magnetic field lines that unleash solar flares.

Built entirely on Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, the study spells out when this "gravitational reconnection" can happen. It also offers a way to measure how fast the theoretical reconnection proceeds, and suggests a change to how gravity and matter trade energy. The process could even play a role in black hole collisions, the researchers suggest.

Magnetic field lines are normally "frozen" into plasma — the hot, electrically charged gas that makes up stars — and carried along wherever it flows. The lines can be stretched and twisted, but not cut. Where this rule breaks down, they can snap and rejoin in a process called magnetic reconnection, releasing pent-up energy in explosive bursts such as solar flares.

"In plasma physics, reconnection has become an essential part of our understanding of how magnetic fields reorganize and exchange energy with matter," Luca Comisso, an astrophysicist at Columbia University and first author of the study, told Live Science via email. "Could something similar be true for gravity?"

"Gravity and magnetism describe very different aspects of nature, so there's no obvious reason to expect them to behave alike," Comisso said. "But when we express Einstein's equations in a particular mathematical form, some of the same principles that govern magnetic fields also emerge in gravity. We wanted to understand whether those similarities extended to reconnection itself."

Comisso and study co-author Felipe Asenjo, a physicist at Adolfo Ibáñez University in Chile, used a mathematical framework known as the tetrad formulation. "Einstein's theory describes gravity through the geometry of space-time," Comisso explained. But in the tetrad formulation, "certain aspects of gravity can be expressed through quantities resembling electric and magnetic fields."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a prior study published in the journal Physical Review Letters earlier this year, the researchers applied this framework to gravity. That study suggested that gravitational fields can form two-dimensional structures called gravitational field sheets. Of the sheets' two dimensions, one stretches through space and the other through time — so each sheet is the trail a line leaves as time passes. A snapshot at any instant therefore catches each sheet as a line, akin to the field lines drawn around a magnet. And, like magnetic field lines frozen into a plasma, "under certain conditions, these sheets evolve without breaking or changing how they are connected," Comisso said.

An illustration depicting the sun’s magnetic field lines over an image taken by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. When magnetic loops get stretched to their limit, they snap and reconnect, triggering solar flares.

In the new study, published Oct. 28 in the journal Physical Review D, the researchers found that this is not always the case. "Gravitational field sheets can break and reconnect in a different arrangement, much like magnetic field lines do in plasmas," Comisso said.

The researchers showed that breaking the frozen-in rule doesn't, by itself, guarantee reconnection. Sometimes, the sheets merely slip relative to the flow that carries them, staying intact because they remain frozen into a different flow. Genuine reconnection happens only when no such alternative flow exists.

"We also derived equations describing how quickly this reconnection can occur and how it can affect the transfer of energy and momentum," Comisso said. In general relativity, gravity and matter can trade energy and momentum, with only their combined total conserved. The study shows that reconnection changes the local rate of that exchange.

Reconnection also alters gravitational helicity, the gravitational counterpart of a quantity that measures how twisted and interlinked magnetic field lines are. Frozen-in sheets keep their helicity fixed, but reconnection can create or destroy it.

The findings don't require new physics. "Everything follows from Einstein's general relativity," Comisso said.

"Einstein developed his theory more than a century ago, and it has passed an extraordinary number of experimental tests," he added. "Yet even after more than a century, there are still new insights to be gained from those same equations."

What could trigger gravitational reconnection in nature remains an open question. Among the candidates the researchers suggested are the singularities thought to lurk at the hearts of black holes and the combined effect of gravitational ripples that are too small to track individually. Quantum effects linked to Hawking radiation ‪—‬ the faint glow that black holes are predicted to emit ‪—‬ could also play a part.

"We're still at the beginning, but one of the most interesting possibilities is that gravitational reconnection could play a role in extreme events, such as the merger of two black holes or the collision of neutron stars," Comisso said. "These are environments where gravity is extremely strong and the geometry of spacetime changes dramatically."

Such collisions send out ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, which detectors such as LIGO (the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) have been recording since 2015. "We'd like to understand whether gravitational reconnection could contribute to transferring energy, and whether it might leave a recognizable signature in gravitational waves," Comisso added. "We don't know the answers yet, but these are questions that we can now begin to investigate."

Comisso, L., & Asenjo, F. A. (2026). Reconnection of gravitational fields. Physical Review. D., 114(8). https://doi.org/10.1103/lmqy-pf9k

#6397. Gut bacteria plays a huge role in vaccine side effects

Gut bacteria that make a protein called flagellin keep low-grade inflammation going, and the people carrying more of them ran a fever.

For some people, a COVID shot means a night of chills and a headache. Others barely notice theirs, and the split holds, dose after dose. To some, this has always looked like luck.

Researchers have now found part of the reason, and it was in the gut before the needle went in. Certain bacteria there build whip-like tails out of a protein that the immune system reads as a warning.

People whose gut bacteria made more of that protein were the ones who ran a fever.

Kelsey Huus and her colleagues at the Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen followed 171 healthy adults in Germany through an mRNA vaccination against SARS-CoV-2.

In people they can only show that gut microbes and fever go together, so they tested cause in mice and in human gut cells grown in a dish.

If gut bacteria set the risk of a fever, that risk may be something a person can change, though that has not been shown in people.

In an interview with Earth.com, Ruth Ley, the study’s senior author, said the bigger idea isn’t really about vaccines at all.

“More broadly, I think the interesting idea coming from the study is that the gut microbiome helps set our baseline inflammatory ‘immune tone,'” she said. “That could potentially be relevant well beyond vaccination.”

Participants took their own temperature three times a day for two weeks, before and after their shot, and wrote every reading in a diary. The diaries came to 7,079 readings from 171 people.

The median was 97.7°F (36.5°C), which is below the 98.6°F (37°C) most of us were taught to expect.

Instead of using a clinical cutoff, the team compared each person against their own normal for that hour of the day.

Anyone whose temperature climbed 1.4°F (0.8°C) or more above their own baseline counted as fever-high. That line left 72 people above it and 99 below.

People who said earlier doses had given them a fever ran hot here too. The two groups also differed on a stool test for gut inflammation. This was higher in the fever-high group two weeks after the shot and tilted the same way beforehand.

Many gut bacteria grow whip-like tails to move around. Those tails are built from a protein the immune system treats as a sign that bacteria are on the move. The protein is called flagellin.

The team read the RNA in each stool sample to see which bacterial genes were switched on. In the fever-high group the flagellin genes were running harder, before the vaccine as well as after. Those gut microbiomes carried a wider variety of flagellins to start with.

One genus accounted for most of that. Waltera, a member of the Lachnospiraceae family, made 67.2 percent of the flagellins that were more active in fever-high people. The family as a whole made 76.3 percent.

That genus was also the only one reliably more common in the fever-high group.

The same thing turned up in a second group of people. Among 1,014 Canadian adults in the CHILD Cohort Study who answered questions about side effects after a SARS-CoV-2 vaccine, the ones who reported any had more Waltera in their stool.

Measuring flagellin isn’t the same as showing it does something, so the team ran two experiments.

First they grew human colon cells in a dish and bathed them in stool extracts from the participants. Extracts from fever-high people pushed those cells to release more of an inflammatory signal, and the amount tracked how much active flagellin each sample held.

Then they transplanted human microbiomes into germ-free mice and vaccinated them. A mouse with an inflammatory reaction doesn’t run a fever. Its temperature drops instead.

Mice carrying a fever-high person’s gut bacteria dropped further, and how far they dropped tracked the fever that person had run.

Mice bred without the two receptors that detect flagellin still reacted, though less, so flagellin carries part of the signal and something else carries the rest.

The animal work was done at Georgia State University, and the gut cells and the additive cultures were handled with Institut Pasteur in Paris.

Diet changed the same thing. In culture, the common thickener carboxymethylcellulose helped Waltera grow, and raised the amount of inflammatory flagellin it made.

In tanks seeded with stool from two donors, that thickener on its own barely shifted those bacteria. A mix of it and 13 other additives of the kind that go into ultra-processed foods raised both the bacteria and the flagellin they made.

Mice fed a Western-style diet, high in fat and low in fiber, reacted harder to the vaccine than mice on standard chow. Their temperatures dropped further, and a day later they carried more of a second inflammatory signal.

Among the 171 people, 46 said they ate a plant-based diet. Temperatures rose less in that group than in the 125 omnivores.

The gap held even after the team adjusted for gender, age, body mass index, dose, fever medication, earlier fevers and starting antibody levels.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her most, Ley pointed at how fast diet changed what the bacteria produced in the laboratory. “That gives us a plausible way in which diet could influence inflammatory immune tone through the microbiome,” she said.

None of this reached the part of the vaccine response that protects you. Fever-high participants carried somewhat higher antibody levels before and after their shot, but the booster lifted both groups by the same amount,. Diet made no difference either.

The mice ended up in the same place. Germ-free animals given fever-high or fever-low microbiomes finished with matching antibody levels, and the ones that cannot detect flagellin made antibodies anyway.

“This suggests that the mechanisms that make someone feel ill after vaccination are at least partly distinct from those responsible for generating protective antibodies,” Ley told Earth.com.

The human diet data are the thinnest part of the work. Participants picked from broad categories rather than filling in a food diary, and Ley said as much herself.

“But the dietary findings in people are much more preliminary: we only have broad, self-reported dietary categories, so we cannot conclude that diet caused the differences in fever that we observed,” she said.

The group was narrow by design. Everyone was a healthy adult between 18 and 40, with a median age of 25 years. Anyone immunocompromised, living with a gut disorder or recently on antibiotics was left out.

Huus and her co-authors wrote that their definitions of fever were built for research and may not meet the standard for a clinical diagnosis.

Ley said she wants to know first whether the same pattern shows up in other groups of people.

“One important next step is to determine whether the relationship between microbial flagellin and vaccine reactions holds across different populations, age groups and vaccines,” she said.

Her team also wants to know whether a person’s inflammatory tone can be shifted at all, which would take a controlled diet trial.

For now, a fever after a shot may say as much about the gut it arrives in as about the shot itself.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6394. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

#6393. The saying ‘blind as a bat’ is completely wrong, according to a new study

New research shows that bats have tiny eyes to stabilize vision and combine sight with echolocation to navigate and hunt.

Bats are not blind. They have small eyes with very sensitive vision that lets them see in conditions people might call pitch black, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS).

Their eyesight is not as sharp or as colorful as ours, but it does not need to be. The agency likens bat vision to that of “a dark-adapted Mr. Magoo,” the cartoon character known for his poor eyesight.

Recent studies show how much bats use that vision. A 2026 study from Johns Hopkins University found that bats move their eyes to steady their view, overturning an assumption that dates to 1942.

Optometrist Gordon Walls made the claim in his 1942 book The Vertebrate Eye and Its Adaptive Radiation. He wrote that the eyes of small nocturnal mammals, bats among them, “never move even reflexively.”

The idea went untested for more than 80 years. It fit a view of bats as animals that rely on echolocation for nearly all of their navigation.

Kathleen Cullen is the Raj and Neera Singh Professor of Biomedical Engineering at Johns Hopkins. Her team tested the assumption in Seba’s short-tailed bats, Carollia perspicillata.

The team included Grace Capshaw, Dimitri Skandalis and Cynthia F. Moss of Johns Hopkins, along with Hui Ho Vanessa Chang of Inha University. Chang carried out the work as a Ph.D. student in Cullen’s lab.

The researchers moved visual patterns in front of the bats and recorded the animals’ eye responses.

The bats tracked the moving patterns across a range of about 10 degrees in each direction. The eyes slowly followed the motion, then quickly snapped back to center.

That response, called the optokinetic reflex, helps keep an image steady on the retina. It resembled the response of mice and other mammals.

The team also passively rotated the bats’ heads from side to side. Unlike in most mammals, their eyes barely moved in response to that rotation.

The bats did show strong eye responses driven by the otolith organs, which sense gravity and linear motion, when rotated on a tilted axis.

Micro-CT scans showed that their inner-ear balance organs are nearly identical to those of mice, which responded strongly to head rotation. The difference appears to lie in how the brain uses those signals.

The authors propose that the system is specialized for active flight. It stays relatively quiet when a bat is at rest but likely engages during rapid, acrobatic maneuvers.

The eye-movement experiments compared four bats with six mice.

“This study shows that the brain’s solutions to navigation are more flexible than we assumed,” Cullen said.

“Even in an animal as specialized as the bat, multiple senses are integrated in ways that depend on behavior and environment,” she added.

“In bats, we see that this integration is dynamically tuned depending on context,” she explained. “The same is true for humans.”

Understanding how the brain combines these senses could help in treating balance disorders and in designing better rehabilitation and assistive technologies, according to Cullen.

A 2025 study of wild common noctules, Nyctalus noctula, showed vision at work during hunting. Researchers from the Leibniz Institute for Zoo and Wildlife Research (Leibniz-IZW) and Aarhus University tagged 21 bats with miniature sensors.

The tags recorded light levels, echolocation calls and movements. When the bats hunted in brighter conditions, they cut their calling rate in half and called up to 7 decibels louder.

They also flapped harder and flew faster. Average foraging speed rose from about 11.6 mph (5.2 meters per second) in the dark to about 17.7 mph (7.9 meters per second) in light.

Prey capture was about 50 percent faster in lit conditions. When the bats were simply commuting, their calls and flight did not change with brightness.

Laura Stidsholt, the study’s first author, was a postdoctoral researcher at the Leibniz-IZW and is now at Aarhus University.

“We show that the bats reduce the acoustic tracking of their prey when enough light is available as complementary sensory information,” Stidsholt said.

Calling less did not make the bats worse hunters. “At the same time, we were able to reveal that this happens not at the expense of hunting efficiency,” Stidsholt pointed out.

Insect-eating bats are very active in the early hours of the night, at dusk. They can presumably combine echolocation and vision most efficiently then, in the view of Christian Voigt, head of the Leibniz-IZW Department of Evolutionary Ecology.

“Our study provides the first direct evidence that bats rely on multisensory information when foraging, highlighting the remarkable flexibility of their sensory systems,” Voigt noted.

The Johns Hopkins team reaches a similar conclusion. Its results challenge the view that bats rely almost entirely on sound, showing instead that they combine vision and sonar to make split-second decisions.

The study was published in the journal Current Biology.

#6392. Memory tests may miss clues hidden in the time it takes to answer

Memory tests may reveal more than correct answers, as slower responses in older adults could signal subtle changes.

Getting an answer right on a memory test is usually considered a good sign. But what if it takes someone much longer to reach that answer?

That delay might tell us something important.

New research suggests that the time older adults take to answer memory questions could reveal subtle changes in how their brains work, even when they manage to give the right answers.

Anglia Ruskin University researchers found that older adults with possible mild cognitive impairment (MCI) answered some memory questions more slowly than healthy older adults. Distractions made the gap clearer.

MCI affects memory and thinking beyond normal aging, but people can usually manage daily life. Some later develop dementia, though many do not.

Professor Shahina Pardhan, who worked on the study, thinks measuring answer times alongside memory scores could help doctors spot early changes. The idea needs more testing.

The study brought together 115 people. There were 34 young adults, aged 18 to 30, and 61 healthy older adults, aged 55 or above.

Another 20 older adults had scored below the cutoff on at least one of two standard screening tests. The team placed them in an at-risk group for mild cognitive impairment, or MCI.

Nobody in that group had a confirmed MCI diagnosis. Those screening results were a reason to investigate, rather than proof that someone had the condition.

People with MCI have more difficulty with memory and thinking than normal aging would explain, but can usually get on with everyday activities. Some later develop dementia, though many do not.

In the word task, people watched two or four color words appear briefly in different places. The computer then showed one again and asked whether it was in the place where they’d seen it before.

Participants had to remember each word’s location while ignoring its ink color.

A mismatch between a color word and its ink, such as “red” printed in blue, can create interference known as the Stroop effect.

The at-risk group got more answers wrong than both the young and healthy older groups.

With two words to remember, they took longer to answer too; the timing differences between groups weren’t clear enough to rule out chance with four words.

There was no instruction to hurry. Participants were asked to get the answers right, while the computer recorded how long each response took.

In the arrow task, an arrow could point in one direction while moving in another. For example, it might point left and move right, or point and move in the same direction.

At the time they saw an arrow, participants didn’t know what they’d be asked to recall about it.

Either its movement or the way it pointed could come up in the question, so they had to remember both.

It wasn’t possible to pick one detail and ignore the other throughout the task, as they could with ink color.

Remembering both might have changed how they dealt with a mismatch, the researchers suggested.

With two arrows to remember or four, the at-risk group answered more slowly than healthy older adults.

But unlike the two other groups, they showed no clear extra delay when an arrow’s movement and pointing direction clashed.

Healthy older adults did about as well as young adults with the words, but made more mistakes with the arrows. The two groups answered at similar speeds on the arrow task despite that difference in mistakes.

For young adults and healthy older adults, wrong answers on the word test generally took longer than correct ones.

Perhaps they hesitated because they weren’t sure, the researchers suggested.

The 20 at-risk participants took roughly the same time whether they were right or wrong. One possibility is that they were less aware of making mistakes, though the study didn’t establish this.

And that pattern didn’t carry over to the arrows. All three groups took longer when they gave a wrong answer on that task.

For both older groups, words in matching ink were quicker to deal with than words in clashing ink. Young adults showed little measurable change between those conditions.

The at-risk participants were slowest of all on the conflicting word trials.

They were also slower than healthy older adults on the arrows overall, so the lack of an extra delay from mismatched arrows wasn’t evidence of better performance.

Answers to the word task weren’t clearly less accurate when the ink clashed.

That’s something an accuracy score alone could miss: people could still choose correctly, while needing more time to do it.

The researchers suggested that ignoring the ink took extra effort.

Age can make it harder to keep unwanted information out, and memory and thinking problems may add to that difficulty.

Researchers tested participants once, so they couldn’t link slower answers to later memory loss or MCI. The at-risk group included only 20 people, none with a confirmed MCI diagnosis.

The reasons for the delays remain unclear, and the lab tasks may not reflect everyday memory.

Larger studies following people over time, including adults with diagnosed MCI, could help test the approach.

Professor Shahina Pardhan, who worked on the study, sees promise in measuring response times.

“These findings suggest that measuring reaction times alongside memory performance could help clinicians detect subtle cognitive changes at an earlier stage,” Pardhan said.

“As populations continue to age and dementia becomes an increasing public health challenge, there is a growing need for sensitive, accessible tools that can identify people at greater risk before symptoms become more severe.”

The full study was published in the journal Brain Sciences.

In this excerpt from "This is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth," author and physicist Christophe Galfard explores the way 19th century scientists were starting to use thermodynamics to understand just how old Earth is.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the 1950s, American geochemist Clair Patterson presented findings that showed Earth is around 4.55 billion years old. His evidence was based on lead isotopic analysis that he used to calculate the age of the Canyon Diablo meteorite, which was discovered in Arizona in 1891. That result is now widely accepted as the age of our planet, but the buildup to this discovery was a long time coming.

Earth's true age was a subject of much debate among scientists in the 19th century. And rather than geologists taking the helm, it was physicists who realized that this giant ball of rock we live on must be far older than the thousands of years that had been assumed in prior centuries. Their main reasoning was heat.

In this excerpt from "This Is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth" (University of Chicago Press/Picador, 2026), author and physicist Christophe Galfard looks at the progression among scientists who were coming to realize that thermodynamics was an essential piece of this long-standing puzzle.

Some two and a half centuries ago, the foremost experts on scientific matters knew a thing or two about heat. They knew, for instance, how heat could be transferred from one place to another. A new science was about to emerge out of this knowledge, a science called thermodynamics, which means "movements of heat" in Greek.

Thermodynamics isn't a force. It is more like a guidebook, a set of rules that apply to large

numbers of particles when they come together. It gives us, humans, a way to understand how particles behave when there is a lot of them without needing to refer to each one of them individually. It shows us how properties that don't exist on their own arise when many particles are together. It deals with these things we call emergent phenomena, such as heat and pressure, and which [Philip] Anderson's "More Is Different" tried to make sense of.

Understanding the dynamics of heat meant a lot to nineteenth-century scientists — so much so that many saw in it the roots of a philosophy so universal and powerful that they thought it should guide us through all our lives. Some even went as far as believing that heat was the source of eternal life. A prominent scientist became so convinced that this was the case that he locked himself up in his house and overheated it, thus shielding himself from all mortal diseases (ageing and death included). The experience was a true torture for the occasional guests who came to visit him, not to mention his wife, who had to endure it day and night.

The scientist held fast to his belief, though, piling on layer after layer of clothing to keep himself ever warmer. Unfortunately, the bulk made it difficult to move, and he eventually missed a step on his own staircase and died from the fall.

As a scientific discipline, thermodynamics was born with a book written in 1824 by a 27-year-old French physicist named Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot, who, as he explained how heat could produce work, told everyone how the steam engine worked.

Lord Kelvin giving a lecture at Glasgow University in 1899.

With Carnot's vision, the way hot objects cool down began to be understood, raising hopes that the resolution of one particular problem might be imminent: the determination of the Earth's age. Were we to somehow guess how hot our planet was at birth, thermodynamics could then be used to tell us how much time had gone by for it to have cooled to its present temperature. Many scientists tried it, keen to be the first one to nail the true age of our world.

Considering our planet in all its complexity to be far too difficult, simplifications were in order, and British physicist William Thomson shot first by picturing our world as a ball. A very simple, rock-solid ball made of pretty much the same stuff throughout, from surface to core. No ocean, no mountain, just a smooth ball the size of the Earth. He then calculated how long it would take it to cool down from being red hot to its present temperature, and declared that the Earth was something between 40 and 400 million years old.

Refining his calculations, he then announced that the world was 100 million years old, before settling for 40 million again.

Thomson's result does not correspond to the true age of the Earth, but it was a start. It was the result of a model, an attempt at figuring out something about our world using still-to-be-refined laws, and mathematical sense. What was more problematic was that no one dared question his results. Even as it shifted from one paper to another, the age of the Earth given by Thomson was always greeted as the right one. A reason for this is that at the end of the nineteenth century Thomson had become Lord Kelvin.

The same Kelvin after whom the Kelvin unit of absolute temperature is named. A scientific superstar who had the power to undo, in a snap of fingers, the career of anyone who disagreed with him.

Lord Kelvin was a physicist, not a geologist, so geologists could have questioned his work, but they didn't. In fact, they weren't bothered. Many of them back then believed that being a geologist was all about intuition and proper English, a language they deemed far more efficient than mathematical gibberish.

That being said, and however wrong the results, Kelvin's calculations were beautiful, giving whoever wanted to think about the problem of the age of the Earth a way forward, which is exactly what one of his former students, Northern Irishman John Perry, did. He thought that Kelvin had overlooked something. As a man of science talking to his former mentor (and job provider), Perry explained his vision to Kelvin but was ignored.

John Perry, a student of Kelvin's, who realized Earth was billions of years old — and that its mantle was a liquid, not a solid.

Still, he published his thoughts in Nature. But again, the article was ignored. Not just by Kelvin, but by the scientific community at large, including geologists.

It would have saved us all quite a bit of time had this not been the case, because Perry not only found a much more correct way to picture the Earth and estimate its age than Kelvin had, but he also found the source of the power that makes our planet's continents drift.

In his model, Perry didn't picture the Earth to be uniformly the same from surface to core as Kelvin had. Instead, he modelled the Earth's interior as being divided into three regions: a metallic core at its centre, a solid crust at its surface, and a mantle that lay in between the two. Rather unexpectedly, Perry didn't envision the mantle as everyone else would have; he believed that it didn't behave like the solid rock it was, but as a liquid.

No wonder his former master didn't take him seriously. However, he pictured the mantle behaving like a liquid only when considered over long periods of time. Sandwiched between a hot core and a colder crust that very much looked like a lid, he believed the mantle had no choice but to behave just like water does in a heated pan, with the hottest parts at the bottom rising and cooling before diving back down and rising up again, in repeated loops, albeit in extremely slow motion. This type of movement is called convection, and it happens in solids, too.

If he was right, there would be two immediate consequences. The first one was that the time it would take for our planet's surface to cool down from red hot to its current temperature could now be far longer than Kelvin had estimated. The lid and the convection patterns prevented our planet from quickly radiating away all its energy into space, so we were now inhabiting an Earth that could be as old as 2 or 3 billion years. Maybe even more. Such timescales were unheard of in the scientific community. Back then, no one knew that the universe itself was 13.8 billion years old. They knew next to nothing.

The second consequence of Perry's model was that the mantle's circular movements underneath the crust could drag the crust itself via friction. The solid surface of our world would then move, and split into pieces that would drift, and collide, and plunge underneath — or slide above — one another. Where they collided, mountain ranges would rise, like the Alps, the Himalayas, the Rockies . . . Where they split apart, rifts would appear, probably in the middle of oceans, along ridges . . . just like [Marie] Tharp had found.

Nowadays, these broken pieces of our planet's surface have all been mapped. They are our world's plates and their movements through time are called plate tectonics. Today, most of us have heard about plate tectonics. Back then, however, no one had, and if very few people remember Perry today, it is because another scientific breakthrough made the estimation of the age of the Earth much easier and precise, showing us that our world isn't 2 or 3 billion years old, as Perry suggested, but precisely 4.567 billion, give or take a few million.

#6388. AI can copy how people write online, but one thing still gives it away

Nine AI models learned the shape of online replies in a new test, but AI-generated text still gave itself away through emotion and tone.

Ask a chatbot to write a reply to a post the way a regular person would, and the result usually reads fine. That is the problem. A reply can sound natural to a human reader and still be nothing like what a real person would have written.

A computer program, however, told the two apart 70 to 80 percent of the time.

Nicolò Pagan of the University of Zurich and Petter Törnberg of the University of Amsterdam ran that test on nine AI language models. The raw material was real conversations from X, Bluesky, and Reddit.

The models learned the shape of online talk well enough. What they couldn’t fake was the feeling behind it, and the harder the team pushed them to sound human, the less they said what the human had actually said.

The stakes go beyond spotting bots. Social scientists have started using these models as stand-ins for people, simulating how crowds might react to a news feed or a policy.

The study asks whether the stand-ins behave like the people they replace.

The team collected replies that real users had posted to real messages. The sample held 275 users on X, 492 on Reddit’s politics forum, and 59 groups of similar accounts on Bluesky, with 20 replies each.

Then they asked each AI model to write its own reply to the same original message, in the style of the same user.

A separate program was trained to look at a reply and guess whether a person or a model wrote it. If the AI replies were indistinguishable from the human ones, that guess would be right about half the time, no better than a coin toss.

The nine models came from six families, including Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and DeepSeek. Most were small by today’s standards, and one, Llama 3.1 70B, was far larger.

All were open-weight models that researchers can run on their own computers, so the biggest commercial chatbots, such as ChatGPT, were not tested.

Christopher Bail of Duke University and Christopher Barrie of New York University and the University of Oxford were co-authors on the research publication.

The standard setup feeds the model a written description of the user’s personality and interests. With that alone, the detector was right at least 87 percent of the time for every model on every platform.

The clearest tells were how long the replies ran, how long the words were, and how toxic the language was. The models wrote longer replies than people did, and the versions tuned to be helpful assistants produced less hostile language than real users.

Several models also stuffed replies with hashtags and mentions that real users almost never used.

On the emotional side, the replies differed from human ones in categories such as positive emotion, negative emotion, and the language of speaking and communicating.

In an interview with Earth.com, Törnberg said the most surprising part was how stubborn those gaps were. “What surprised me most was how persistent the differences were,” he said.

“So in a sense, the models can become quite good at reproducing the form of online conversation, but less so with its feeling.”

The team tried five ways of coaching the models, each one adding to the last.

These were a bare prompt, a prompt with a persona description, ten examples of the user’s past replies, relevant snippets pulled from the user’s history and, finally, retraining the model itself on the user’s writing.

The persona description, which is how most researchers currently do this, made little difference and sometimes made the replies easier to spot. Retraining was unpredictable, and for several models it made detection easier.

The two simplest moves worked best. Showing the model ten real examples cut the detector’s accuracy between about 2 and 10 percent. Adding the user’s past context cut another 2 to 3 percent.

Even the best combinations left the detector right 70 to 80 percent of the time. The bigger model was no better at passing than the small ones, and models tuned to be helpful assistants were generally worse than their raw counterparts.

“I would not assume that newer models will necessarily be better models of human behavior,” Törnberg told Earth.com. He said the training that makes a model helpful and well behaved may be the same training that makes its language less like real human communication.

The study’s second measure asked whether the AI-generated text meant the same thing as the reply the human actually wrote. The team scored that by converting both replies into numbers that capture meaning and comparing them.

The coaching that made replies harder to detect also moved them slightly further from the human reply’s meaning on every platform. The models were learning to write like a person in general, not to say what that person would say.

Next, each model wrote 20 candidate replies, and the team picked one in two ways. Choosing the reply that best matched the human’s meaning roughly doubled the similarity score but did not reliably make the reply harder to detect.

Choosing the reply most likely to fool the detector trimmed its accuracy by 5 to 10 points but left the meaning no closer. The two methods picked the same reply only 5 to 10 percent of the time, about what chance would give.

Asked by Earth.com what else stood out, Törnberg pointed to that trade-off. The team could make replies harder to tell from human writing, he said, but doing so often made them less similar in meaning to what the real person wrote.

Every message in the dataset had only one real human reply, so the meaning score measured closeness to that one reply, not whether the AI’s reply was a reasonable one.

On X, the comparison between two humans answering the same post rested on only 18 pairs, which the authors treated as exploratory.

The models also saw less of each conversation than the human replying had seen. And the detector was more likely to flag a real person as a bot than to miss a bot.

Whether future models close the gap is an open question, the authors wrote, and their test is built to keep asking it. Even a model that passed every statistical check, they added, would not necessarily hold the attitudes behind a human reply.

Törnberg said the fix for researchers is to validate a simulation against real human behavior in the specific setting being studied, rather than trust that it sounds right.

And getting the feeling right, the authors wrote, may take new training goals that target emotional expression directly instead of copying style.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6387. A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Mice that ate lots of fiber had far less particles accumulate in the body

A diet that includes high-fiber foods, like these vegetables, might come with a surprise benefit. Fiber could help carry nanoplastics out of the body, suggests a new study in mice.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

#6385. Even remote wildlife can’t escape microplastics in their blood

Scientists found microplastics in the blood of wild tapirs and giant anteaters in Brazil, including animals living far from human development.

As the afternoon sun began to fade over Brazil’s countryside, a team of researchers drove along dusty dirt roads searching for giant anteaters.

Two spotters rode in the back of the truck, scanning the landscape for signs of movement. When they spotted an anteater, the team approached on foot with two long-handled nets.

Capturing the animal usually took about a minute, but the information gathered would help answer a much bigger question: How far has plastic pollution spread into the natural world?

The researchers were investigating whether wild animals living closer to human activity had more microplastics in their blood.

Their findings revealed a clear connection between human disturbance and plastic exposure.

But one discovery was particularly concerning.

Even in Brazil’s remote Pantanal, the world’s largest tropical wetland, every animal sampled had microplastics in its blood, despite living more than 40 miles (65 kilometers) from the nearest development.

The results suggest that plastic pollution is reaching wildlife even in places that appear largely untouched by humans.

Scientists had widely assumed a connection between human activity and plastic in wildlife.

To test it, the researchers needed several records for the same animals, namely blood samples, GPS movements and detailed maps of human disturbance.

Study co-author Justin Calabrese of the Center for Advanced Systems Understanding (CASUS) described the difficulty of getting all those records together.

“Such integrated datasets simply did not exist,” Calabrese said.

Marcia de Almeida Monteiro Melo Ferraz and Michael Noonan, both at the University of British Columbia Okanagan, conceived the study.

Teams from two long-running conservation programs in Brazil did the fieldwork.

From February 2021 to November 2022, those teams collected blood from 26 lowland tapirs and 21 giant anteaters.

The animals lived at a soy farm on the Amazon’s deforestation frontier, farmland in the Cerrado savanna and a cattle ranch in the Pantanal.

For the anteaters, the work took place near two federal highways, where the Anteaters and Highways Project studies collisions between vehicles and wildlife.

Each blood sample went into a glass tube, which the field team sealed with aluminum foil to prevent contamination.

To record where the animals went, adult tapirs wore GPS collars that logged an hourly position. The anteaters wore GPS trackers as well.

Once in the lab, each sample went through a chemical treatment to break down the blood. The team collected the solids left behind on a filter.

Raman spectroscopy then identified the materials from the way they scattered light from a laser.

When the team had checked all 47 blood samples, 43 contained microplastics. The particles averaged about 0.0004 inches (10 micrometers) in length.

Pieces of that size need a microscope to be seen.

Counts for individual animals ran from zero to more than 1,200 particles in a milliliter of blood. The average for all the animals was about 74, and a milliliter is roughly a fifth of a teaspoon.

For comparison, the average fell within the range already reported in human blood by other studies using spectroscopy.

The tapirs had about 99 particles per milliliter on average and the anteaters about 43. The difference between the species was not statistically significant.

GPS records provided more than 440,000 locations, allowing researchers to map the home ranges of 40 animals.

To describe the land within those areas the researchers used the Human Footprint Index.

This global map has scores running from zero for undisturbed land up to 50 for the most heavily modified.

An animal did not need to live across uniformly disturbed land for a link to appear.

The team found more particles in blood when the most heavily modified spot in an animal’s range had a higher footprint score.

Average footprint scores across entire home ranges were not significantly associated with microplastic levels.

The distance comparisons also pointed to less plastic in animals living farther from development, which here meant urban areas, mines and power plants.

The same was true of animals living farther from waste management facilities.

Calabrese said the paper “is the first to demonstrate this linkage for terrestrial mammals,” meaning mammals that live on land.

The researchers also checked how much the highest values influenced the findings. They ran each test again without the animals making up the top 10% for that measure.

For the distance tests, that meant leaving out the animals living farthest away.

After that check the footprint link remained, while neither distance link was still statistically significant.

Animals with more farmland in their home ranges did not have higher microplastic levels in their blood.

The authors suggested that farmland may add less direct exposure to microplastics than other kinds of human disturbance.

The types of plastic offered another comparison between sites, with differences the authors described as consistent with local land use.

Animals at the Amazon farm carried more polyamide, the main material in fishing nets and ropes, than animals on Cerrado farmland.

The Cerrado animals had more PVC, a material used in irrigation pipes, than animals in the Pantanal.

The authors described the site comparisons as case studies, with uneven numbers of animals at each site.

For the animals at the cattle ranch in the Pantanal, the distance from the nearest waste facility was about 70 miles (112 kilometers). Each of them still carried microplastics in its blood.

The researchers also obtained a value of about 10 particles per milliliter of blood from their model for land with a footprint score of zero.

The authors suggested that the value may partly reflect limitations of the model.

Even so, they wrote that direct contact with land changed by people was unlikely to be the only route into wildlife.

The authors identified wind and water as likely routes carrying microplastics into remote habitats. Cities, industry and farms supply airborne microplastics that may settle far away.

Runoff, rivers and seasonal floods provide ways for particles to move far from their sources as well.

Microplastics in the water and sediment of the Pantanal were already known from previous studies.

The highest measurements in those studies came from places near rivers flowing out of urban areas.

This observational study found associations between human disturbance and microplastic levels in blood, but it cannot establish cause and effect.

The researchers had a single blood sample from each animal. Their method could not identify particles smaller than about 0.00004 inches (one micrometer).

Future studies could collect blood, soil and water samples from the same locations to help trace the particles’ sources.

The team did not collect those environmental samples and could not yet match the plastic in blood to its source.

The measurements also concern the amount of plastic, without examining its effects on the health of these wild animals. Laboratory experiments have shown that microplastics can harm animals.

For the years 2001 to 2020, the increase in Brazil’s average footprint score was 42%, whereas the worldwide increase was 26%.

Thus, as land development continues, the authors suggested that the plastic levels in land animals would continue to increase.

They described keeping wildlife farther from development and waste facilities as a possible way to lower the amount the animals carry.

The study is published in the journal Nature.
