#6384. Dancing may shape how the brain responds to other people’s emotions

Ballet dancers show different brain responses to emotional faces, without identifying emotions more accurately than people without training.

Ballet dancers spend years training their bodies to move with precision.

A new study suggests that the same training is also linked to how the brain responds when a dancer sees fear or happiness on someone’s face.

When ballet dancers looked at photos of fearful, happy, and neutral faces, their brain activity differed from that of people with no dance training.

The differences appeared in brain areas that process vision and in areas that process touch.

Beatriz Calvo-Merino worked with lead author Vasiliki Meletaki and Bettina Forster at City St George’s, University of London’s Centre for Cognition and Neuroscience.

“The impact of dance expertise goes beyond movement and taps into social perception mechanisms, such as face processing and emotions,” said Calvo-Merino.

The team compared 26 professional or trainee ballet dancers with 26 people of similar age and sex who had no dance experience.

The dancers had been dancing for about 17 years on average.

Both groups judged the emotions about equally well, but their brain signals differed in timing and pattern.

Earlier brain-scanning studies, including work by Calvo-Merino, found increased activity in the brains of expert dancers when they watched familiar dance movements.

Nearly all of that research looked at how dancers perceive movement and bodies, the authors wrote.

The team used faces to test whether dancers’ brains also differ in other, everyday kinds of perception.

The test is based on an idea about emotion.

According to this idea, people perceive someone else’s emotion partly through their own body’s sense of that emotion, and not through vision alone.

Researchers describe this as an embodied view of emotion.

Earlier experiments found that the brain area receiving touch and movement signals from the body is involved when people look at emotional faces. That area is the somatosensory cortex.

Professional dancers develop a refined awareness of their own bodies through long, precise training, the authors wrote.

Dance training might also refine the body’s part in perceiving emotion, the team reasoned. If so, dancers’ brains should respond differently to emotional faces as well as to dance.

Each volunteer wore a cap fitted with 64 electrodes. The electrodes recorded the brain’s electrical activity, a method called EEG.

The faces came from a photo collection called the Karolinska Directed Emotional Faces. The team used 60 black-and-white photos, half of them male faces.

Each face stayed on screen for 600 milliseconds, a little over half a second.

In one task, a question about emotion sometimes followed a face, such as “Is s/he fearful?” In the other task, used as a comparison, the question asked whether the face was male or female.

Half of the time, a blunt-tipped device gave a brief touch to the tip of the volunteer’s left index finger.

The touch came 105 milliseconds after a face appeared, and volunteers were told to ignore it.

The touch served as a probe. The team recorded the brain’s response to a face with a touch and to a face alone, then subtracted the second recording from the first.

The subtraction helped isolate the brain’s response to touch. Differences between facial expressions could then indicate that emotional processing was influencing that response.

In the dancers, the touch response differed between fearful and neutral faces at the earliest stage the team analyzed.

That stage was about 143 to 173 milliseconds after the face appeared, less than a fifth of a second.

The response to happy faces didn’t differ from the response to neutral faces at that stage. The early effect was specific to fearful expressions, the authors wrote.

In non-dancers, the touch response didn’t differ by emotion at that first stage.

Their touch responses did differ by emotion at later stages, but at a narrower set of recording sites than in dancers.

“What is particularly interesting is that dance expertise appears to influence how the somatosensory cortex responds to emotions expressed by others,” Forster said.

“This suggests that our own bodily experiences can shape how the brain processes other people’s emotions, providing further evidence for the embodied nature of emotion perception.”

Electrodes over the visual areas at the back of the head recorded a second set of differences.

One difference appeared between about 150 and 200 milliseconds after a face came on screen. In dancers, visual responses to neutral faces differed from responses to both fearful and happy faces.

In non-dancers, visual responses at that stage were different for each of the three expressions. Those differences were also stronger on the right side of the brain, a pattern that earlier face studies have typically reported.

In dancers, the differences were spread across both sides. The authors called the two patterns distinct styles of telling emotions apart.

Both groups processed fearful faces in a distinct way. The authors linked that result to the priority the brain is known to give fear.

The authors also wrote, as an anecdote, that fear is an important tool in dance training. Dancers learn to feel comfortable performing in front of an audience, for example.

The study found no clear advantage in dancers’ ability to identify facial emotions.

During the recordings, dancers answered 94% of the emotion questions correctly. Non-dancers answered 95% of them correctly, a gap too small to rule out chance.

Dancers did score higher on a questionnaire about awareness of signals from inside the body. Their average score was 3.69, compared with 2.71 for non-dancers.

Body awareness may be part of how dancers process other people’s emotions, the authors suggested. They proposed exploring that relationship further.

Each group had 26 people, a size chosen to match earlier studies. The authors sugg that future studies should calculate in advance how many participants they need.

Scalp recordings also couldn’t show precisely where in the brain the differing touch responses arose.

The study compared the two groups at a single point in time, so it can’t show how the differences developed.

The next question is whether the brain differences are accompanied by differences in behavior.

Future studies could add behavioral tests of emotion recognition, the authors wrote.

New studies could also explore how the touch area’s response to emotion changes across stages of dance training, from advanced trainees to professional performers.

The full study was published in the journal Cerebral Cortex.

The new Peerium architecture aims to power hyper-efficient computers capable of training AI models with up to 40 trillion parameters.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Engineers in China have built a new computer architecture they say can one day make up to a million artificial intelligence (AI) chips work as one. For comparison, Elon Musk's AI company, SpaceXAI (soon to be SpaceXSI), describes its Colossus cluster as the world's most powerful AI training system, comprising 200,000 interconnected chips.

Traditionally, the AI chips used to train foundation models are housed in separate servers and communicate over a network to share data and divide workloads. But the new architecture, Peerium, uses a high-speed interconnect system designed to maintain efficient communication between chips across multiple racks, even as the number of chips scales into the hundreds of thousands.

Huawei unveiled the new architecture Sept. 17 at the company's annual CONNECT conference.

Representatives from Huawei said in a statement that computers powered by Peerium could train models with up to 40 trillion parameters. For comparison, competing hardware, like GB200 NVL72 from NVIDIA and CS-3 from Cerebras, have reported training at the trillion-parameter scale, rather than the tens-of-trillions.

"Over the next two years, there will be roughly 6 or 7 frontier AI labs in China, and all will aim at training foundation language models of sizes ranging from 10 to 40 trillion parameters," Liao Heng, chief scientist for Huawei's chip design arm HiSilicon, told the Associated Press. "So you need such a scale of infrastructure to train these models."

Peerium's performance relies on three elements: nested parallelism, unified memory addressing, and peer-to-peer interconnects, Huawei representatives said in the statement.

Nested parallelism allows workloads to be broken into smaller tasks and organized across hierarchical groups of chips that work in parallel. It's similar to how a company breaks down work into departments and then smaller teams, all of which coordinate their efforts toward a common goal. Unified memory addressing allows processors to access memory across other servers, as opposed to only that attached to the processor's own server. Peer-to-peer interconnects allow components to communicate more directly with one another, rather than relying on an intermediary.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

All three principles are designed to make more efficient use of computing resources so that a single system can coordinate larger numbers of chips to handle demanding AI workloads.

According to Huawei, existing interconnect technologies — which link processors and servers to enable them to communicate — cannot support the Peerium architecture at the scale it envisages. For instance, NVIDIA uses NVLink for communication within racks and InfiniBand for communication between racks. The inter-rack communication bandwidth in this setup is 200GB per second, Eric Xu, Huawei's rotating chairman, told the AP.

"With such a low inter-rack communications bandwidth, there is no way you can make one million processors work as one computer," he said.

Huawei instead developed its own interconnect technology, UnifiedBus, which the company says delivers inter-rack communications bandwidth of up to 800GB per second.

"When one million processors work as one computer, this lays the foundation for better and more efficient AI training and inference," Xu added. "Therefore, I see UnifiedBus as the path for the future AI era. I believe, in the years to come, other players would certainly follow suit."

Alongside Peerium, Huawei also announced the Atlas 950 SuperPoD, a computing system built on Peerium and powered by more than 8,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT AI accelerator chips.

Xu said testing for AI training is underway on these SuperPoDs and that results show that they use their available computing power for AI training more efficiently than AI computing clusters that aren’t based on Peerium and UnifiedBus.

Huawei expects to begin supplying the SuperPoDs by early next year, at the latest, before its SuperClusters, which link multiple SuperPoDs to form a larger AI computing system, based on Peerium, eventually come online. Representatives said that one SuperCluster with 256,000 computing cards — hardware modules that add processing capacity — is currently being deployed and tested.

Models with large numbers of parameters demand greater computing resources and infrastructure, which isn't always desirable as it increases costs. In the summer, researchers used an IBM quantum computer to reduce the perplexity of Meta's Llama 3.1 8B language model — a measure of how well it predicts the next word or token — while keeping the number of parameters almost unchanged.

#6381. Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Semaglutide helped repair blood vessels and reduce inflammation in the kidneys, a study finds

A patient undergoes hemodialysis, a process that filters waste from blood when the kidneys can’t. A new study shows how the popular weight loss drug semaglutide can help repair damaged kidneys.

Maria Symchych-Navrotska/iStock/Getty Images Plus

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

V. Perkovic et al. Effects of semaglutide on chronic kidney disease in patients with type 2 diabetes. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. doi: 10.1056/NEJMoa2403347

#6378. Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The decrease is probably temporary and a result of high gas prices from the Iran war

The disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Iran has raised oil and gas prices around the world. According to new projections, those higher fuel prices will decrease global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel burning in 2026 by about 0.16 gigatons from 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

A man's appendix had to be removed, but not for dangerous inflammation, as you might expect.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: The man went to the emergency room because he had a sharp pain in his lower-right abdomen.

What happened next: When doctors examined the man, the type of pain and the location of his discomfort suggested that he might have appendicitis, or inflammation of the appendix.

Appendicitis can be dangerous because it can cause the appendix to burst and release bacteria from the bowels into the abdominal cavity, thereby infecting the cavity's lining. This infection, called peritonitis, can spread to the bloodstream and cause the life-threatening condition sepsis, which kicks the immune system into overdrive.

Even though the patient had acute pain in his lower-right abdomen, he did not show signs of peritonitis, such as fever, nausea, symptoms of dehydration and an elevated heart rate, according to a report of his case. His doctors then performed abdominal ultrasound scans and found that the man's abdominal organs, including the appendix, appeared normal, with no signs of inflammation.

The report's authors did not include details about the man's treatment after this examination. But eight months later, he was still in pain and returned to the hospital for further evaluation, they noted.

The diagnosis: This time, when medical personnel questioned the man, he recalled that approximately 15 years earlier, he had accidentally swallowed a piece of a long bone containing edible marrow. The report does not mention if the man sought treatment immediately after swallowing this bone.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

At this second visit, doctors performed an abdominal X-ray and found a round object near the upper right of the man's pelvis. It measured about an inch (2.5 centimeters) long and a little over an inch (3 cm) wide.

According to a subsequent CT scan, the object contained bone tissue and was near the appendix. When the doctors looked inside the patient's abdomen with a laparoscope — a long, flexible tool with a camera at one end — they saw that the appendix was enlarged.

The treatment: Surgeons performed a laparoscopic appendectomy, which uses small incisions in the abdomen to insert instruments for removing the appendix. Inside the appendix was a hardened mass of fecal matter, called a fecaloma, which surrounded a long bone.

The organ's muscular walls had been stretched out by the mass, but there were no signs of inflammation. No complications developed after the surgery, and the patient was discharged two days later. The report does not describe any follow-up visits or treatments.

The appendix (orange) is a small, thin pouch of tissue attached to the colon.

What makes the case unique: It's relatively uncommon for people to accidentally swallow something indigestible and then require a medical visit for it. In the United States annually, about 120,000 people — roughly 90% of whom are children — are treated for ingesting foreign objects, and most of the objects are swallowed accidentally. Most commonly, the adults requiring treatment have ingested jewelry, while children are more likely to swallow coins, toys and batteries.

Typically, small, swallowed items pass harmlessly through the intestines within 48 hours; less than 1% require surgical intervention. Some objects, however, need immediate attention. For example, sharp items can tear the esophagus or puncture digestive organs. Batteries are hazardous if swallowed, as they contain corrosive acid that can leak into the gut. And small magnets are a big risk, especially if two or more are involved, since they may stick together through intestinal walls, which can tear holes in tissues or cause blockages and contortions in the intestines.

Swallowed foreign bodies rarely affect the appendix. Whether they enter the organ depends on the size of the opening into the appendix where it connects to the colon (which can vary between individuals), the dimensions of the ingested object, and the appendix's position in the body at the time. These objects cause approximately 0.005% cases of appendicitis, according to the man's case report. Such items recovered by surgeons through appendectomies include pieces of coal, nails, bits of enamel and glass, shells, dental crowns and bullets.

When a foreign body migrates to the appendix, it typically generates appendicitis within a few months, at most. However, this is not always the case. One report described a man who had eaten pigeons as a child and discovered more than 30 years later that he had 27 lead shot pellets in his appendix. Despite containing these pellets from the birds' flesh, his appendix was not inflamed.

"It is therefore possible, although rare, that a foreign body in the appendix even after many years (in our case, 15 years) does not lead to an authentic appendicitis either histologically or clinically," the authors of the marrowbone case report wrote.

They added that their patient was the first record in the scientific literature of a sizable bone lingering inside an appendix for more than a decade without causing significant inflammation. His pain was likely caused by physical shifting of the hard mass. His experience presented "a unique clinical picture," the doctors wrote.

"This case could offer a possible diagnostic and therapeutic option for appropriately treating patients with foreign bodies within the appendix," they said.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

#6374. Could a nuclear blast save Earth from an asteroid? Good aim will mean everything

Computer simulations reveal how an asteroid’s shape could affect efforts to push it off course with X-rays from a nearby nuclear blast.

A nuclear blast set off near a dangerous asteroid could, in theory, push it away from Earth. But if the asteroid has a lumpy, uneven shape, how hard it gets pushed depends on which side the blast hits.

In new computer tests, hitting one side of an oddly shaped asteroid instead of another gave it nearly five times as much push.

So a real defense mission could depend on knowing an asteroid’s shape before anyone chooses where to aim.

Nathan Moore, a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories, led the research. “We expected aim to matter,” he said. “What surprised us was how much.”

No asteroid was blasted for this work. The team ran every test in computer simulations, using the shapes of real asteroids.

In this kind of defense, a nuclear device would go off some distance from the asteroid, not on it.

The blast sends out a burst of X-rays that heats one side of the asteroid and turns part of its surface into vapor. That vapor rushes off into space, and the pressure it puts on the surface pushes the asteroid the other way.

The goal is to push the asteroid, not smash it. Breaking it apart could turn one big threat into smaller pieces that could still be deadly.

A nuclear blast is a different approach from crashing a spacecraft into an asteroid, which NASA’s DART mission tested in 2022.

Moore has worked on this question since a 2024 experiment at Sandia’s Z machine, a lab device that produces intense bursts of X-rays.

That experiment showed for the first time that X-rays could push a small piece of asteroid material.

Next, he wanted to know how a full-size asteroid would respond. Most researchers had treated asteroids as perfect spheres because that made the math easier, he said.

Real asteroids have irregular shapes that a perfect sphere cannot capture.

“You can make estimates that way, but asteroids come in all kinds of odd, lumpy shapes,” Moore said.

He found a way forward in a colleague’s work on how objects in space give off gas.

“I think we had an aha moment when we realized we could do this,” he said. “No more spheres. We would be able to model deflection for any asteroid.”

Moore built the new model by joining two computer programs that Sandia already used for very different jobs.

One usually simulates fast, high-energy events, such as experiments on the Z machine. The other usually handles weak forces that change slowly, like the drag the solar wind puts on a satellite.

In the new model, the first program works out how the X-rays heat the surface and turn part of it to gas.

The second follows that gas as it spreads across the asteroid’s real 3D shape, and it calculates the pressure on every part of the surface.

“The key innovation here was figuring out how to combine the two simulation approaches,” Moore said.

He also pointed to speed. “Our new algorithm is over 1,600 times faster, which was critical to this breakthrough,” he said. “With the old models, computers just couldn’t handle it.”

To use the model, the team loads in an asteroid’s shape, which can come from detailed 3D images taken by passing spacecraft.

They then set the size of the blast, how far away it goes off, and which side it hits.

The program maps how much of each part of the surface turns to vapor. From that map, it works out how hard the asteroid gets pushed and how fast it spins afterward.

The team tested the model on three real asteroids with very different shapes. Bennu is the asteroid NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft sampled in 2020. The other two were Itokawa and Golevka.

For each one, the researchers tried blasts at close range and farther away. They also changed which way the asteroid was facing when the X-rays arrived.

In the simulations, orienting Bennu at its most favorable angle, instead of its worst, gave it up to nearly twice as much push.

The difference was larger for the other two, at up to nearly four times for Itokawa and five times for Golevka.

In one simulation, the blast changed an asteroid’s speed by about 0.15 inch (3.9 millimeters) per second from one angle. From another angle, it was only about 0.03 inch (0.8 millimeter) per second.

The asteroid and the blast were the same both times, and only the side facing the X-rays was different.

The aim also affected how fast an asteroid spun after the blast. For one asteroid, the change in its spin rate varied 17-fold depending on which side faced the blast.

“Our study shows how important it is to aim carefully,” Moore said. “Pick the right side and you win. Guess wrong and it could be a bad day.”

To run the model, the team needs a fairly accurate picture of an asteroid’s shape from every side. In a real emergency, there might not be time to get one.

Placing a nuclear device at the right distance, on the right side of an asteroid speeding through space, would also be hard.

Another unknown is what happens to the whole asteroid.

“Right now, our computer model only considers breakup of rocks on the surface,” he said. “We can’t predict breakup of the entire asteroid body accurately yet.”

When the researchers applied the blast pressures to a loose, Itokawa-like pile of boulders, the rock thrown off was lopsided, just like the vapor.

Predicting whether a whole asteroid breaks apart will take more research and better modeling tools. An X-ray blast would set off many effects at once, and those effects could change one another.

That full calculation is what Moore and other scientists are working toward.

The full study was published in the journal Icarus.

#6373. Plant roots have a clever way to tell good and bad fungi apart, even though they both give off the exact same molecules

Good and bad fungi release the exact same chemical signal but plant roots still know which one is dangerous

A fungus growing on a crop sounds like bad news, but not all fungi are harmful. Plants also rely on helpful fungi to take up nutrients through their roots.

Attackers and partners alike are built from the same material, a sugar chain called chitin. Fragments of it end up in the soil whenever a fungus grows or breaks down.

A new study shows how a receptor on legume roots sorts those fragments by length.

Receptors tightly grip long chitin chains, the kind that come with a fungal attack, and raise the alarm. Short ones, the kind that partner fungi shed, barely register.

Kira Gysel and Kasper Røjkjær Andersen of the Department of Molecular Biology and Genetics at Aarhus University in Denmark led the work.

Simon Boje Hansen and Henriette Rübsam are the first authors, with co-authors at the University of Copenhagen and the French research center CERMAV. The experiments were done in two small legumes used as laboratory models, not in crops.

In an interview with Earth.com, Gysel said the puzzle was that chitin looks the same along its whole length.

“It’s the same sugar repeated, like a string of identical beads, with nothing to tell one part of the chain from another,” she said.

Chitin is the main building block of a fungal cell wall. When a fungus grows or gets broken down, pieces of the chain of different lengths end up in the soil. Roots read these fragments of fungi to keep track of the microbes around them.

Long fragments usually come with an attack and, in legumes, they set off a much stronger defense than short ones. Short fragments come with the helpful fungi that plug into roots and exchange nutrients with the plant.

How a root told the two apart was the open question.

The team produced the outer part of a root receptor called CHIP13 and tested how hard it holds chitin chains of different lengths. It held an eight-sugar chain more than 1,000 times more tightly than a five-sugar chain.

Then they froze the receptor into crystals with the long chain attached and mapped it, atom by atom.

The receptor holds the chain at three points. Two are standard chitin-binding pockets found in related receptors. The third sits between them, and the team named it the bridge domain, because it spans the middle of the chain.

Gysel told Earth.com that the structure answered the question at a glance.

“CHIP13 holds the chain at three main contact points, and the central one, the bridge domain, is what coordinates binding of the long chitin chain,” Gysel said.

“Only chains long enough to reach all three are held tightly and can activate the plant’s immune response. It’s really a molecular measuring tape.”

Swapping out two amino acids near the bridge cut the receptor’s grip 100-fold. In a second legume, barrel medic, mutant plants given a version of the matching receptor with the same two swaps didn’t regain their response to chitin.

Legume roots also need a second receptor, CERK6, to respond to chitin, and CERK6 can barely hold chitin at all. Boje Hansen said that had been a puzzle.

“It turns out the two receptors split the work: one recognizes the signal, the other passes it on. Neither can do the job alone,” he said.

In leaf cells engineered to carry both receptors, CHIP13 pulled in CERK6 only once chitin was bound. The weakened version of CHIP13 didn’t recruit it at all.

The team’s model is a pair of CHIP13 receptors holding chitin and recruiting two CERK6 partners, which then pass the alarm into the cell.

To test the receptors in a living plant without altering its genes, the team raised nanobodies – tiny antibody-like proteins made by immunizing a llama – that plug each receptor’s chitin-binding site.

They soaked intact seedlings of the model legume Lotus japonicus in them. When asked by Earth.com what else about the research stood out, Gysel pointed to that experiment.

“We simply applied them to plants from the outside, and we weren’t sure it would work at all,” she said. “We thought the plant cell wall would block the nanobodies from reaching the receptors on the surface of the plant cells.”

The nanobodies reached the receptors. Seedlings treated with the CERK6 blocker responded to chitin about as weakly as plants missing that gene, and the CHIP13 blocker cut the response sharply too.

Both legumes are laboratory models, and the measuring tape hasn’t been checked in a crop. The bridge domain can be predicted in many related receptors across higher plants, but a predicted domain isn’t a tested one.

Gysel said the two receptors are only a glimpse of a larger immune system. Plants use many related receptors to monitor soil microbes. How those receptors work together, and whether others read signals by length, is what her group wants to find out next.

The stakes she described are agricultural. Strengthening the chitin alarm could make crops more resistant to fungal disease, but only if it doesn’t also fire at the fungi the roots depend on.

“Knowing how the long chitin chains are read helps us improve crops without tipping the balance, so we don’t weaken their defenses to make room for helpful fungi, or the other way around,” Gysel said.

Which crop receptors carry a bridge domain, and whether they measure chitin the same way, is the next thing to check.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6372. Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A century-old pollution trail leads scientists back to Montana mining

At the turn of the twentieth century, the Anaconda Smelter in Montana spewed arsenic into the air — those heavy metal particles that are now trapped in Arctic ice cores.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting company in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

Joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

In the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

The largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a big hint, McConnell says, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, says Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”

Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data showed, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell says, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”

These new findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”

J.R. McConnell et al. Widespread North American pollution and health impacts from early 20th C copper production. Nature Sustainability. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41893-026-01975-9

#6370. SpaceX goes for a Starship double catch

On Monday, Nov. 9, SpaceX is targeting 10:03 p.m. EST to launch USSF-627 on a Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 4 East at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. The mission is a classified payload for the U.S. Space Force. The booster will aim for the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.

On Wednesday, Nov. 11, the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) is targeting 6:40 a.m. EST for a Long March 2D launch from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been disclosed.

On Thursday, Nov. 12, ExPace, a subsidiary of the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation (CASIC), is targeting 2:50 p.m. EST for a Kuaizhou 11 launch from Jiuquan, according to Next Spaceflight. Kuaizhou 11 is a solid-fueled rocket designed for fast-turnaround launches of small satellites. Its payload is also undisclosed.

Later Thursday, Nov. 12, SpaceX returns to Vandenberg at 11:23 p.m. EST for USSF-317, another classified Space Force mission on a Falcon 9. The booster is again slated to land on Of Course I Still Love You.

On Friday, Nov. 13, United Launch Alliance (ULA) is targeting 12:54 p.m. EST for Vulcan Leo 1 from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The launch ends a nine-month grounding that followed a nozzle failure during February’s USSF-87 mission; ULA says the boosters now carry a redesigned nozzle. It’s also Vulcan’s first flight for Amazon, carrying 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the broadband megaconstellation formerly known as Project Kuiper.

Later Friday, Nov. 13, SpaceX opens a 75-minute window at 5:45 p.m. EST for Starship Flight 15 from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas. It’s the 15th test flight of the company’s reusable megarocket and only its second trip to orbit, after Flight 14’s success in September. About six and a half minutes after liftoff, the Super Heavy booster should return to the launch tower and be caught by its chopstick arms. SpaceX has made that catch before with the rocket’s V1 and V2 boosters, but this will be a first for the new V3 booster. The upper stage, called Ship, will continue to orbit and release 26 of SpaceX’s next-generation Starlink V3 satellites as it did in September.

You can watch the launch live on SpaceX’s website.

The next day, SpaceX will try to catch Ship, too. Until now, Ship’s test flights have ended with a practice landing at sea where the vehicle flips upright, fires its engines, and sets down on the water. This time, after about 14 orbits at roughly 171 miles (275 km) up — a flight of more than 22 hours — Ship must run that same landing maneuver over Starbase, settling into the tower’s arms instead.

SpaceX says Ship will head for the tower only if flight controllers confirm that every system it needs for the catch is prepared. If not, the company can bring Ship down at preplanned spots in the Pacific, with checks built into the flight for splashdowns near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile. If the catch works, Starship will become the first orbital rocket ever recovered in full. On Saturday, Nov. 14, Rocket Lab is targeting 12:30 a.m. EST for The Mountain God Rises, the 100th launch of its Electron rocket, from Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula. Electron will deploy a QPS-SAR satellite for the Japanese company iQPS in Rocket Lab’s 11th dedicated launch for the operator. The iQPS constellation uses synthetic aperture radar (SAR), bouncing microwaves off the ground to map Earth’s surface even through rain, smoke, and total darkness.

On Monday, Nov. 2, Rocket Lab launched The Sea God Surveys from New Zealand at 11:41 a.m. EST, delivering another QPS-SAR radar satellite for iQPS. It was Electron’s 99th flight and Rocket Lab’s 10th mission for the Japanese operator. That evening at 7:15 p.m. EST, CAS Space’s Kinetica 2 lifted off from Jiuquan and placed 18 satellites for China’s SpaceSail broadband constellation in polar orbit. It was only the rocket’s second flight, following its debut in March.

On Thursday, Nov. 5, a Long March 2C launched from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center in southwestern China with three Yaogan 51 satellites. Yaogan is the label China gives its government Earth-observation spacecraft, which are widely believed to perform military reconnaissance.

Friday, Nov. 6, brought two launches about an hour apart. Galactic Energy’s Ceres 2 put four satellites in orbit from Jiuquan at 6:37 p.m. EST. Then, after several days of delays, SpaceX launched the classified USSF-432 mission from Vandenberg at 7:48 p.m. EST, landing the booster on Of Course I Still Love You.

On Saturday, Nov. 7, Russia’s Aerospace Forces launched a Soyuz-2.1b from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome in northern Russia. The payload is believed to be a GLONASS satellite for Russia’s version of GPS. The week closed Sunday, Nov. 8, when a Long March 12 lifted off from the Wenchang commercial launch site on Hainan Island at 3:24 p.m. EST, carrying nine more satellites for Guowang, China’s state-run internet megaconstellation.

On Friday, Nov. 20, CASC is targeting 6:00 a.m. EST for a Long March 8A launch from Wenchang, likely carrying another batch of Guowang satellites, according to Next Spaceflight.

On Tuesday, Nov. 24, at 2:00 a.m. EST, a Long March 12 is slated to fly another Guowang group from Wenchang, according to Next Spaceflight.

#6369. Can more snow save Antarctica’s ice? A new study weighs the odds

Antarctica is likely to lose ice through 2100 even with sharp emissions cuts, as extra snowfall struggles to offset losses driven by warmer seas.

Predicting how much ice Antarctica will lose means weighing two competing effects. Warmer air can bring more snow, adding ice to the continent, while warmer seawater speeds ice loss along its edges.

A new study suggests Antarctica is very likely to lose ice overall by 2100, even if emissions fall sharply.

Extra snowfall is very unlikely to make up for the ice that the ocean removes, and the researchers found that very high emissions would probably lead to greater losses.

The author leading the work is Yucheng Lin, an assistant professor at City University of Hong Kong, who worked with colleagues in Australia, New Zealand, the United States and the United Kingdom.

Their study used a machine-learning program to examine existing computer simulations of the Antarctic Ice Sheet and check them against the satellite record.

The Antarctic Ice Sheet contains enough ice to raise global sea level by about 190 feet (57.9 meters), and its losses accounted for roughly 10% of global sea-level rise between 2006 and 2018.

How much emissions will alter the losses during this century has been a source of disagreement, something the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change drew attention to in its 2021 assessment.

One large international comparison included some simulations in which Antarctica lowered sea level by more than 2.8 inches (seven centimeters) by 2100 and others in which it raised sea level by more than 15.7 inches (40 centimeters).

All of these simulations assumed very high emissions.

Making these models involves deciding how easily ice slides over the bedrock beneath it and how quickly seawater melts floating ice from below. It also requires choosing a climate model to provide the warming projections.

Different research groups make different choices about each of these things.

Counting each model equally also gives more influence to choices that appear in more models, Lin’s team wrote, and those common choices may not be the ones that best fit observations.

Their approach was to compare the choices with Antarctica’s recent behavior.

The team used 340 simulations produced by 16 research groups. They recorded the modeling choices behind each simulation, then trained a machine-learning program to predict how those choices affected the results.

Running a full ice-sheet simulation takes a lot of computing power, but the trained program could turn out about 30,000 projections a second on a laptop, so the team could try 100,000 combinations.

To judge them, the researchers used the GRACE satellite record, which showed an average loss of about 174 billion tons (158 billion metric tons) of ice a year from 2002 to 2021.

They gave greater importance to combinations that produced losses close to what the satellites measured, reducing the range of projected sea-level rise by 30% to 42% depending on the emissions scenario.

The middle estimate moved up by 15% to 25% as a result.

With the satellite record helping to decide how much importance each combination received, the estimated chance of Antarctica losing ice overall by 2100 went from 80% to 92% in the lowest-emissions case.

For very high emissions, the researchers put the chance of an overall loss at no less than 95%.

The middle estimate for Antarctica’s contribution to sea-level rise by 2100 was 1.3 inches (3.4 centimeters) under the lowest emissions and 2.4 inches (6.1 centimeters) under very high emissions.

There was an 89% chance of very high emissions producing more sea-level rise from Antarctica than the lowest-emissions scenario, the team calculated.

“We have to transform our energy system to cut every emission we can, and we must do it quickly,” Lin said.

One set of simulations showed how much the extra snow could matter, with a net gain of ice in Antarctica even though the climate model they used produced the most warming this century out of the five models in the study.

More snowfall, together with only modest warming of the surrounding ocean, accounted for the gain. But it did not last in simulations that continued beyond 2100, when losses to the ocean overtook the added snow.

For people planning infrastructure that has to last a long time, including nuclear power stations, the team also examined the outcomes with the most sea-level rise.

These were the top 1% under very high emissions, and all still matched the satellite record.

In this selected group the middle estimate for Antarctica’s contribution by 2100 was 6.2 inches (15.7 centimeters), with one in 20 outcomes exceeding 10 inches (25.4 centimeters).

The sea was the starting point in these simulations, with strong warming melting the floating ice shelves quickly from below.

Ice on land then moved into the sea faster as the shelves thinned or collapsed and lost their ability to hold it back, particularly where the ice could slide easily over bedrock.

For these highest losses the team was looking at the very high emissions case, which the authors described as increasingly implausible given current climate policies.

Researchers cannot use this program to learn what happens in a process that the original simulations never included.

Among the processes that most simulations leave out are flows of water beneath the ice sheet and a still-debated way in which ice shelves might rapidly collapse, both of which could speed up ice loss, the authors wrote.

The satellite record covers only about 20 years, offering limited insight into processes that have caused little ice loss so far but could become important later.

The researchers stopped their projections at 2100 because the available simulations for the following century are too few to capture the sharper changes that begin then.

Of all the choices researchers make when building these models, the authors identified three that need stronger evidence.

These are how ice slides over bedrock, how ice shelves melt and which climate model is used.

Lin pointed out that researchers have limited resources, so they need to work out which details of an ice model matter most.

The authors suggested collecting new field observations and studying records of past climates to help narrow these choices.

Future simulations that include the missing processes could also provide new data to train the program.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Geoscience.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope could capture images 30% sharper than — and remain operational for twice as long as — initially expected. Researchers say these "remarkable" developments could greatly enhance the volume and quality of the data they will analyze.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is nearing its final destination more than 1 million miles (1.6 million kilometers) from Earth, where it will soon scour the universe for a host of cosmological treasures, including an estimated 100,000 new alien worlds.

But even before its mission truly begins, recent developments suggest the state-of-the-art spacecraft could take better images than — and remain operational for more than twice as long as — initially expected, further delighting already-excited astronomers.

"It is fantastic to learn that Roman is not just reaching its design goals but exceeding them," Eamonn Kerins, an astronomer at the University of Manchester in the U.K. who will help lead one of Roman's major surveys, told Live Science.

Roman is NASA's latest flagship space telescope, following in the footsteps of iconic observatories like the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The $4 billion machine ‪—‬ which is over 42 feet (12.7 meters) long and weighs around the same as a fully grown Tyrannosaurus rex ‪—‬ successfully launched into space on Aug. 30, more than a decade after scientists started building it.

The telescope is now en route to Lagrange point 2 (L2), a fixed point relative to our planet where Earth's gravity and the sun's gravity cancel each other out. There, Roman will join several other important spacecraft, including JWST and the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope.

Roman was launched into space on board one of SpaceX's Falcon heavy rockets. It lifted off Aug. 30 from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

During Roman's journey to L2, which is currently around 85% complete, mission scientists have remotely switched on the telescope's various instruments to test whether they function as expected. So far, this "commissioning process" has gone off without a hitch, and by the time Roman arrives in less than two weeks, it should be ready to snap its first in-depth images of the cosmos.

Researchers were already pumped to see what Roman will be able to do once it is in place and fully switched on. However, that excitement has further intensified in recent weeks, thanks to two postlaunch developments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

First, a series of near-perfect rocket burns, executed during and shortly after launch, saved more than a decade's worth of fuel that can now be used to extend Roman's mission. Second, after remotely adjusting the telescope's mirror, researchers discovered it should be capable of snapping images with around 30% greater detail than engineers predicted.

The team that designed, launched and remotely commissioned the orbital observatory has "done an amazing job" and "their work has ensured that Roman is more than up to the task," Kerins said.

Shortly after Roman arrived in space on board a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket that lifted off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, mission scientists conducted two major burns, or engine firings, which gave the spacecraft enough momentum to escape Earth's orbit and make the journey to L2.

Roman is around the same size as a small truck and was packed into the nose cone of the Falcon Heavy rocket prior to launch.

Thanks to a combination of "exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team" and "brilliant execution by the operations team," these burns were so precise that each one saved up to four years' worth of fuel, Jamie Dunn, director of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, said in a Sept. 14 statement.

On top of this, Roman ended up being much lighter than initially planned, which allowed engineers to pack another four years' worth of fuel into the spacecraft before launch. "Since Roman's [weight] was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed," Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard, said in the statement.

In total, these savings could give Roman an additional 12 years of fuel, which could more than double the mission's planned 10-year lifespan. That means Roman could still be capturing images of the cosmos in 2048.

Given that Roman can collect data up to 1,000 times faster than Hubble, this extended lifespan will greatly enhance the amount of data the new space telescope will be able to capture. "With a 20-year Roman lifetime, we could, in theory, do over 20,000 years of Hubble survey work," Kerins said. "That's a lot of science!"

Roman is now on its way to L2, where the gravity of Earth and the sun cancel out, allowing it to remain in one place without expending much fuel.

This prolonged lifespan will let astronomers compare images of specific objects decades apart — such as expanding nebulas or colliding galaxies — allowing them to detect changes they otherwise might have missed.

It may also let them study objects or phenomena that we haven't even discovered yet, which is particularly exciting, Kerins noted. "The real show-stopper results will be new things we just aren't even thinking about right now," he said. "The possibilities are truly breathtaking."

There is also the chance that Roman's mission could be extended even further, because engineers often find clever ways of making active spacecraft last longer. For example, Hubble is more than two decades past its initial mission parameters, and the recently deceased Swift Observatory lasted 10 times longer than initially predicted before falling back to Earth last week.

Roman's secret weapon is arguably its Wide Field Instrument (WFI), made up of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror, which will capture ultra-detailed images with a field of view roughly 100 times larger than Hubble's.

Roman's WFI consists of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror. It will be capable of capturing images with a field of view 100 times greater than Hubble.

We have already seen the first WFI images — a series of blurry, green dots captured during a test of the instrument's 18 different light detectors ( see below). However, those photos were nothing like what WFI will capture in the future; those images will be so detailed that you would need dozens of high-definition TVs to properly display a single snap in full resolution, Kerins said.

After Roman completes the initial WFI commissioning phase, those images will be around 30% sharper than designers predicted. "All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer who works on Roman at NASA Goddard, said in an Oct. 14 statement. "It's a great outcome."

The improvements were first noticed after the WFI's car-sized mirror was realigned by just one-sixteenth the diameter of a human hair, demonstrating just how intricate the commissioning process has been. "Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," Maxime Rizzo, a WFI systems engineer at NASA Goddard, said in the statement. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."

NASA released Roman's first photos on Sept. 15. Each small square represents one of the telescope's light detectors, and each blurry green spot is a distant star. (This is just a test image and does not represent how the telescope's proper photos will look.)

The improved image quality could really come to the fore during Roman's hunt for potentially habitable exoplanets, which is what Live Science's readers are most excited about for this mission.

Kerins, who is leading the Exoplanet Demographics Working Group for the Transits in the Roman Exoplanets Survey, is particularly excited about this development, but he said it does not necessarily guarantee that Roman will find more exoplanets than initially predicted.

The rest of Roman's commissioning phase is also proceeding as planned.

Roman's coronagraph instrument, which will block out the light from distant stars to allow WFI to spot alien worlds, has passed its main commissioning phase and is working as intended, according to a NASA blog post.

Roman has completed around 85% of its journey to L2 and should arrive at its final destination in the next few weeks. (The timeline in this image is a screenshot from Roman's commissioning process website, captured on Nov. 11.)

Meanwhile, a global network of ground stations, which will receive up to 1.4 terabytes of data from Roman every day, has established contact with the spacecraft and is receiving signals as expected, another blog post revealed.

All of these early wins raise hopes that Roman can have a long and successful career, and are a testament to the years of work that went into designing the spacecraft and planning the mission.

"What we're seeing now with the actual optical performance and estimated lifetime of Roman is just how good that design process has been," Kerins said. "It's a remarkable achievement. I can't wait to see what Roman is going to give us."

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

#6366. The Sky Today on Tuesday, November 10: Seek Saturn’s two-toned moon

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 9: Chase Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS

Challenge yourself to pick up Saturn’s moon Iapetus, which tonight reaches greatest eastern elongation 9.4’ east of the ringed planet. The two-toned moon is tidally locked to its parent world, which means it rotates in time with its orbit. At eastern elongation, Iapetus’ darker hemisphere faces earthward, reducing the moon’s magnitude to nearly 12. This, combined with its distance from Saturn, makes it more of a challenge to find, but you can give it a try if you’ve got a larger scope.

Try around 9 P.M. local time when Saturn is highest, some 50° above the southern horizon. It’s the brightest point of light in this region of the sky, hanging just below Pisces and to the far upper left of Fomalhaut, the brightest star in Piscis Austrinus (much closer to the horizon). Even if you can’t locate Iapetus or don’t have a large scope, Saturn is magnificent through a telescope. Its disk spans 19” and its rings are roughly 43” across, showing off their southern side. You should definitely spot its largest and brightest moon, mid-8th-magnitude Titan, just over 2’ west of the planet. Depending on your scope and when you look, you may also spot at least three other moons: 10th-magnitude Tethys, Dione, and Rhea, closer to the planet. Tethys lies to Saturn’s west, while Rhea and Dione are to the east.

Sunrise: 6:39 A.M.Sunset: 4:48 P.M.Moonrise: 8:15 A.M.Moonset: 5:19 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (4%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Venus reaches a stationary point among the stars of Virgo at 10 A.M. EST on November 11. This brings its retrograde (westward) motion to an end; after today, Venus will begin moving eastward or prograde through the sky, swinging north of Spica.

You can easily catch the bright planet in the eastern sky before dawn. Venus’ brightness has increased over just the past few days, and it now blazes at magnitude –4.7. An hour before sunrise, you’ll easily spot it alongside Spica, standing just to the star’s upper right. Both are 10° high and rising as dawn approaches. Check out Venus through a telescope: its disk shows off a crescent phase just 10% lit, but stretches an impressive 53” in the sky.

Also just becoming visible at this time is Mercury, barely 1.5° above the horizon and glowing at magnitude 1.2. See if you can locate it about 13° east (to the lower left) of Venus, although you’ll need a particularly flat horizon free of trees, buildings, and lights. Mercury, too, rises as twilight brightens, which may make the planet harder to see in the growing light. Try scanning for it with binoculars, although make sure to put them away well before sunrise from your location

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.
